national leadership and coordinated action. This progress must be protected. Sustained preparedness, vigilant surveillance and strong cross-border coordination remain essential to preventing further transmission and strengthening health security across the region,\" Kaseya said.","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr />\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">KAMPALA - \u003Cstrong>Two leading public health institutions have cautioned Uganda against lowering its guard with the latest declaration of an end to the Ebola outbreak, saying the situation in neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to pose a serious threat to regional health security.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The caution was delivered on August 3 during a high-level joint mission visit by the World Health Organisation (WHO) Regional Director for Africa, Prof. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, and the Africa Centres for Disease Control (CDC) director general, Dr. Jean Kaseya, to Kampala.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The two directors met with Vice President Jessica Alupo and health ministry officials to review lessons from Uganda's successful containment of the Ebola Bundibugyo disease outbreak and discuss strengthening regional preparedness. \u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />While commending Uganda's swift response that interrupted transmission, the two leaders stressed that the country's achievement must not lead to complacency as Ebola continues to spread across the border.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/a384777b-944a-4aaf-8f99-74d2eb22ebf9.jpg\" alt=\"Uganda declared the end of its latest Ebola outbreak on July 28, 2026, after the Ministry of Health confirmed there had been no new cases following the recovery and discharge of the last patient.\" width=\"1000\" height=\"595\" />\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\"Uganda has shown what decisive leadership, strong preparedness and community trust can achieve,\" Kaseya said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He said Uganda's response offers valuable lessons for the continent, including the importance of acting early, coordinating national response efforts and involving communities at every stage of an outbreak.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />But Kaseya cautioned that the gains remain at risk, especially with the rising numbers in the neighbouring DRC.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\"We commended Uganda for successfully containing the Ebola outbreak through strong national leadership and coordinated action. This progress must be protected. Sustained preparedness, vigilant surveillance and strong cross-border coordination remain essential to preventing further transmission and strengthening health security across the region,\" he said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />On his part, Prof. Janabi said Uganda's proximity to the ongoing outbreak in eastern DRC means the risk of imported infections remains high despite the country's Ebola-free status.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\"We commended the country's leadership in containing the Ebola outbreak and recognised the dedication of health workers, communities and partners whose efforts helped interrupt transmission. With the outbreak continuing in neighbouring DRC, Uganda is still at risk. Sustained surveillance, readiness and cross-border coordination will be essential to detect and respond rapidly to any new cases,\" Janabi said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/23bd29bf-03a7-4c1c-9537-5592004d834d.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"1000\" height=\"650\" />\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The two leaders reaffirmed the commitment of WHO and Africa CDC to continue supporting Uganda in strengthening its health systems, improving emergency preparedness and promoting regional collaboration to prevent future outbreaks.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Uganda declared the end of its latest Ebola outbreak on July 28, 2026, after the Ministry of Health confirmed there had been no new cases following the recovery and discharge of the last patient.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The outbreak, caused by the Ebola Bundibugyo strain, was contained through rapid case detection, extensive contact tracing, laboratory testing, treatment of confirmed cases, infection prevention measures and intensive community engagement.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Uganda also strengthened surveillance at border points and activated emergency response teams across high-risk districts to minimise the risk of further spread. \u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The response has since attracted regional recognition, with health experts describing it as an example of how early intervention and coordinated leadership can successfully contain deadly infectious disease outbreaks.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Uganda has also extended its expertise beyond its borders following a request from Africa CDC and WHO. Uganda recently deployed more than 80 health professionals to eastern DRC to support efforts to contain the ongoing Ebola outbreak there.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Despite Uganda's success, the two health chiefs said the situation in DRC underscores why preparedness cannot be relaxed. greatest-ever Commonwealth Games boxing campaign during the 1970 edition.","\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>For the first time ever, the Uganda boxing team, The Bombers, failed to win a single medal in a Commonwealth Games edition in which they were fielded.\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>The disappointment is even more painful considering it came in Scotland, where Uganda enjoyed its greatest-ever Commonwealth Games boxing campaign during the 1970 edition.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Then, in 1970 in Edinburgh, the Bombers produced a historic performance, winning five medals, including three golds courtesy of light flyweight James Odwori, lightweight Mohamed Muruli, and heavyweight Benson Masanda. Flyweight Leo Rwabwogo and featherweight Deogratius Musoke added two silver medals to complete Uganda's most successful outing at the Games.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Those five medals propelled Uganda to the top of the boxing medal standings ahead of powerhouses England, Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya—a feat the country has never repeated.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>With those glorious memories in mind, the Bombers returned to Scotland hoping to revive their rich boxing heritage, only to endure their worst Commonwealth Games campaign on record.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Of the six boxers Uganda fielded in Glasgow, five reached the quarterfinals, but none survived the wrath of their opponents.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Heavyweight Abdul Aziz \"Ringo,\" a man who has made headlines in many international media outlets for being the grandson of former Ugandan president Idi Amin, was disqualified after a headbutt against England’s Thomas Damar.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Bombers captain Nuhu \"Muzaata Batteso\" Batte was eliminated by another Briton, Patris Mughalzai, just like light heavyweight Alfred \"Gorilla\" Ojok, who lost to Dimeji Shittu, and flyweight Angel Katushabe, who fell to Ruby White.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Welterweight Emily Nakalema was eliminated by Australia's Eve Bryson, with lightweight Ibrahim Kemis being the only Ugandan boxer to exit in the first round.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>Why the Bombers flopped\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>A barrage of factors has been cited for the Bombers' dismal campaign in Glasgow.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>First of all, there was a poor preparation campaign, as the team never had any residential training camp. The situation would have worsened had city tycoon Hamis Kiggundu not bailed the team out by allowing them to use Hamz Fitness Gym for non-residential training sessions.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Observers say the Uganda Boxing Federation (UBF)'s lack of a clear strategic vision and development system for the team, coupled with chronic underfunding—where UBF currently operates on an annual government allocation of Shs265 million, a budget many believe is insufficient to adequately prepare elite athletes for major international competitions—cost the team dearly.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Additionally, a decline in talent, a poor technical and lacking coaching system, and a lack of luck, where all five Bombers quarterfinalists were drawn against heavyweights, all contributed to their dismal campaign.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>The fact that all six boxers in Glasgow were debutants with no international exposure or build-up fights added salt to an already bleeding wound.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>UBF president Moses Muhangi admitted the team fell short of expectations.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>\"Truthfully, we did not perform as we had anticipated,\" he said. \"We underperformed because we did not prepare well. Secondly, due to limited resources, we failed to organise build-up competitions to fine-tune the team. Luck was also not on our side,\" Muhangi told Vision Sport.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>But Fred Kavuma, Muhangi’s former vice president, went bare-knuckle, placing the blame squarely on the federation's leadership.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>\"I am not surprised the team flopped. What else could you expect after the systems we had in place—such as the National Open Boxing Championships, which used to be the main platform for selecting the national team—were made dysfunctional by the current federation?\" he said.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>WHAT NEXT?\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Despite the disappointing results, Muhangi insists the federation has already begun planning for the future. \"We are going back to the drawing board to see a way forward. All that we are going to do will be in liaison with the National Council of Sports (NCS),\" he said.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Muhangi also revealed that the federation is considering recruiting an experienced foreign coach, preferably from Cuba, to strengthen both the national team and the capacity of local coaches.\u003C/p>\n\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\n\u003Cp>Other priorities include lobbying the government to establish a national boxing gymnasium and a dedicated boxing academy, as well as reviving boxing in schools to rebuild grassroots talent.\u003C/p>","https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/a76858ed-e834-4978-9fc8-e48b97451bc4.jpg",[259,260],"Commonwealth Games","The momentum.","\u003Cp>________________\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">President Yoweri Museveni has reaffirmed Uganda's support for Ambassador Olara Otunnu's candidature for United Nations Secretary-General, using a meeting with representatives of United Nations Security Council member states to rally diplomatic backing for the veteran Ugandan diplomat.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />During the meeting on Monday (August 3) at State House Entebbe, Museveni formally presented Otunnu as Uganda's candidate and urged diplomats to support his bid to lead the world's top multilateral organisation as the selection process gathers momentum.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The President described Otunnu as an experienced statesman whose decades of service within the United Nations have prepared him for the organisation's top office at a time of growing global challenges.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/f670798b-c524-4657-a6e4-2224825317ee.jpg\" alt=\"President Museveni addressing diplomats from the UN Security Council Member States during a meeting on the candidature of Ambassador Olara Otunnu's UN Secretary-General bid. (PPU Photo)\" width=\"1000\" height=\"610\" />\u003Cbr />“He is really the type of person you will need in the UN system because he is very much aligned to it. I therefore hand over Olara Otunnu to you,” President Museveni said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Museveni said he had known Otunnu since their days at Makerere University, where he served as guild president, and praised his diplomatic credentials, including his command of English and French.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />“He speaks English and French very well without a tribal accent, so I hand Ambassador Olara Otunnu to you so that he can brief you himself,” the President added.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The President also cited Uganda's record on regional peace and security, as well as its refugee policy, as strengths that reinforce the country's endorsement of Otunnu's candidature.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />“Uganda's credentials in the UN are many, but the uncontested ones are two: our contribution to regional security—I don't think anybody will say Uganda is not known for that—and our support for refugees. Our candidate comes from that background,” he said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />“Of course, we are also excelling in democracy, although others may have different views, which I will not insist upon. But on refugees and our contribution to regional security, I think everybody will agree.”\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />In his remarks, Amb. Otunnu thanked President Museveni for the Government's endorsement, noting that several members of the Security Council had sought assurances regarding Uganda's commitment to his candidature following previous unsuccessful attempts.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/561f685c-f7a9-4e43-b02a-2adc5b1e8b8f.jpg\" alt=\"President Museveni addressing diplomats from the UN Security Council Member States during a meeting on the candidature of Amb Olara Otunnu's UN Secretary-General bid. (PPU Photo.)\" width=\"1000\" height=\"667\" />\u003Cbr />He said he had informed them that the President was best placed to clarify Uganda's position and expressed gratitude for the opportunity to engage the representatives alongside the Head of State.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Otunnu outlined his distinguished international career, having served as Uganda's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, President of the UN Security Council, Chair of the UN Commission on Human Rights, President of the International Peace Academy (now the International Peace Institute), and United Nations Under-Secretary-General and Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He said his experience spans peace and security, humanitarian affairs, human rights and development, with a leadership approach rooted in consensus-building and dialogue.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />According to Otunnu, preventing conflicts, maintaining international peace, supporting peacebuilding and promoting post-conflict recovery should remain the United Nations' foremost priorities.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He also unveiled his vision for strengthening the effectiveness and credibility of the organisation through institutional reforms aimed at improving efficiency, coordination and accountability.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />On development, Otunnu said the Secretary-General should play a stronger convening role in mobilising long-term financing for developing countries with credible development plans but limited financial resources.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He further called for the United Nations to spearhead global cooperation on emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, by bringing together governments, experts and the private sector to ensure technological advancement benefits all humanity.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Otunnu reaffirmed his commitment to promoting transparency, merit and inclusivity within the United Nations, saying recruitment should reflect the organisation's universal character while maintaining the highest professional standards.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He described the office of the Secretary-General as one founded on moral authority, humility, consensus-building and active engagement with member states in advancing peace, sustainable development and international cooperation.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Representatives of Security Council member states welcomed the opportunity to engage with President Museveni and Amb. Otunnu, outlining the priorities that would guide their respective governments during the Secretary-General selection process.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />They commended Otunnu's distinguished international record and welcomed his emphasis on peace and security, development, human rights, institutional reform and emerging global issues, including artificial intelligence.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The diplomats also acknowledged Uganda's significant contribution to regional peace and security, particularly in the Horn of Africa and the Great Lakes Region, as well as its internationally recognised refugee policy.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Former Prime Minister Dr Ruhakana Rugunda reaffirmed Uganda's determination to secure broad international backing for Ambassador Otunnu's candidature.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />President Museveni announced that Dr Rugunda would lead a Ugandan delegation to engage governments in various capitals as part of Uganda's diplomatic campaign.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />“We are going to send our delegation led by Dr Rugunda to your capitals,” President Museveni said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Rugunda described Otunnu as a distinguished Ugandan statesman whose service at both the national and international levels has prepared him to lead the United Nations.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He noted that Amb. Otunnu has remained an important national leader through his leadership of the Uganda People's Congress and his participation in presidential elections.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/130a93ea-56cd-4765-bdcd-fbc8961ff0b8.jpg\" alt=\"President Yoweri Museveni chats with diplomats from UN Security Council Member States after a meeting on the candidature of Amb Olara Otunnu's (4th R) UN Secretary-General bid. (PPU photo)\" width=\"1000\" height=\"667\" />\u003Cbr />“I am very happy that you have endorsed Ambassador Otunnu. We will give him our full support,” Dr Rugunda said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />He added that Uganda believes the time has come for Ambassador Otunnu to realise his long-held aspiration of serving as Secretary-General of the United Nations.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />“I think now is the time to actualise this long-postponed aspiration,” he said.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />Dr Rugunda also appealed to the diplomats to convey Uganda's message of support to their respective governments.\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />“I hope that the ambassadors will clearly convey the message to their respective governments.”\u003Cbr />\u003Cbr />The meeting was attended by ambassadors representing both permanent and non-permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, including Somalia, Denmark, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Pakistan, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, the United States and other member IT ALSO PLAYS A MAJOR ROLE IN SAFEGUARDING HUMAN HEALTH.","\u003Cp>As Uganda’s livestock sector expands, the health of animals is becoming more closely linked to the livelihoods of millions of farmers, food safety and public health. Behind every healthy herd of cattle, successful poultry farm or thriving livestock enterprise is the need for proper veterinary care provided by trained and regulated professionals. Recognising this importance, the Uganda Veterinary Council (UVC) has continued to strengthen supervision of the veterinary profession by ensuring that all veterinary practitioners and animal health establishments operating in the country are registered and licensed according to the law. Observed annually, World Refugee Day honours the courage and determination of people forced to flee conflict, persecution and violence. This year’s theme, Until Everyone Is Safe, coincides with the 75th anniversary of the 1951 Geneva Convention, the international treaty that established the legal framework for refugee protection The occasion comes at a critical time for Uganda, which hosts more than two million refugees and asylum seekers, making it Africa’s largest refugee-hosting nation and one of the top six globally. Most refugees come from neighbouring South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Rwanda, Burundi and Somalia. South Sudanese account for about 52% of the refugee population, while Congolese make up 33%. More than half of all refugees in Uganda are children. The country has provided refuge for decades. When I last visited and asked why, the answer was simple: “Because others helped us when we needed them, so now we help them.” That message is especially important this World Refugee Day. New figures from UNHCR show that nearly 118 million people worldwide remain forcibly displaced by conflict, violence, persecution and disaster. While the total has fallen slightly for the first time in more than a decade, displacement remains at record levels. One in every 70 people on Earth has been forced from home, and the number of displaced people has almost doubled over the past decade. This is not a story of crises being resolved. It is a story of crises forcing difficult decisions. Millions returned home in 2025, but many did so because they had little choice, not because peace had returned. At the same time, refugee resettlement to wealthy countries has fallen to its lowest level since 2011, asylum backlogs are at record highs and humanitarian funding continues to shrink. Against this backdrop, Uganda offers an example the world should support and emulate. Uganda is Africa’s largest refugee-hosting country, welcoming more than two million refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from Sudan, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Its 2006 Refugee Act remains one of the world’s most progressive refugee frameworks, granting refugees freedom of movement, the right to work, own property and access public services. These are not abstract principles. They are practical policies that enable people fleeing conflict to rebuild their lives and contribute to society. Rather than isolating refugees, Uganda has embraced a model based on inclusion, coexistence and opportunity. While capital is essential, experience has shown that money alone does not build sustainable institutions. What transforms communities is strong leadership, accountable governance and structured systems that inspire trust and discipline. It is on this foundation that the Microfinance Support Centre (MSC) has distinguished itself — not only as a provider of affordable credit, but as a builder of resilient leadership and governance structures within supported savings and credit cooperative organisations (SACCOs) and community groups across the country. Today, thousands of SACCOs supported by MSC are no longer informal associations. They are structured, member-owned financial institutions with elected leaders, functioning committees, regular meetings, transparent accountability systems, and recognised certificates of registration. This transformation is quietly reshaping Uganda’s socioeconomic landscape. MSC recognised early that sustainable financial inclusion requires more than disbursing funds — it requires building institutions. Through structured capacity building, supervision and technical support, MSC has guided SACCOs to have by-laws, constitutions, establish governance organs and comply with regulations and operationalise clear leadership structures. Today, supported SACCOs conduct democratic elections where members elect their executive committees, supervisory committees and credit committees. Forty-five years ago, on that very date in 1981, a group of ordinary villagers in Kikandwa, Luwero, faced death rather than betray their friends and their hopes for freedom. Their executions by government soldiers marked the beginning of what would become Heroes Day, a national occasion to honour those who sacrificed everything during the bush war and beyond. This year’s commemorations come with a more restrained feel, shaped by health concerns and a practical focus on safety, yet the story of that fateful morning still carries power to inspire new generations. The road to Heroes Day started in the uncertain days of early 1981. Uganda was tired. After years of political turmoil, President Milton Obote’s government had lost the trust of many, especially in rural areas, where people felt squeezed by oppression and unfair rule. On February 6, Yoweri Museveni and a small group of fighters slipped into the bush to launch a guerrilla war aimed at changing that reality. In a statement, the Commander of UPDF 1 Division, Brig. Gen. Fred Mwesigye, speaking on behalf of the Chief of Defence Forces (CDF), Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, commended the troops for their dedication and contributions to national security and peace beyond Uganda’s borders. “You are going on a mission, not for leisure. Remain focused, work as a team and adhere strictly to the guidance of your commanders,” Mwesigye emphasised. He cautioned the troops against indiscipline, including alcohol abuse and negligence, while on duty, noting that such actions could undermine both individual safety and the UPDF’s long-standing reputation. Battle Group XLVII is the latest unit to be deployed to Somalia under the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) framework, where the group will join other UPDF contingents in efforts to stabilise the region and support peace-building initiatives. Mwesigye reminded the troops that they carry the image of Uganda and the UPDF, urging them to uphold the force’s legacy. For context, BG 47 means that since 2007, when the UPDF was first deployed in Mogadishu, 47 battle groups have served there. Each BG consists of about 1,500 soldiers or two battalions. For decades, traders operating along Uganda’s inland waters depended on privately owned vessels to transport goods to neighbouring countries. Now, they own a cargo boat, making it the first locally owned community cargo vessel operating from a Ugandan landing site. The development is already improving the economic prospects of residents by enabling them to transport goods across Lake Albert to the DR Congo at lower costs and with greater reliability. The cargo boat was acquired through the Local Economic Growth Support (LEGS), a flagship programme designed to accelerate local economic development through the Integrated Rural Development (IRD) Model, with support from the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) and the Lives and Livelihoods Fund (LLF). The oldest higher institution of learning in East Africa has been ranked the top university in East Africa. It is followed by the University of Nairobi in second position. In Africa, it is ranked 7th. From research and innovation to PhDs and the largest enrolment, Makerere remains at the summit of a pack of 343 universities within the East African Community. Rankings conducted by EduRank and Webometrics, both reputable research houses, place Makerere University in the lead, followed by Kampala International University and Mbarara University of Science and Technology (MUST) in second and third position, respectively. Whilst the two research houses gree on the top three positions, they differ in the subsequent numbers from fourth position to tenth. Edu-Rank places Kyambogo University in fourth position, Gulu University in fifth position, with Uganda Christian University (UCU) and Uganda Martyrs University  (UMU) coming in sixth and seventh, respectively. On the other hand, Webometrics places Uganda Management Institute in fourth position, while Kyambogo, UMU and Gulu are ranked fifth, sixth and seventh, respectively. The positions of Ugandan universities according to Edu-Rank are based on its 2025 report, while those of Webometrics are based on the January 2026 report. According to EduRank.org, the institution ranks a total of 14,131 universities across 183 countries, utilising the world's largest scholarly papers database, with 119,627,370 scientific publications and 3,164,054,493 citations, to rank universities across 246 research topics. According to EduRank, the overall rankings incorporate non-academic prominence and alumni popularity indicators, as well as information drawn from official university websites regarding the latest enrolment figures. Feeding an average of 60,000 officers and soldiers was a major challenge. Yet the army owned vast tracts of fertile land around its barracks, including Hima in Kasese, Kabamba in Mubende, Kyankwanzi, Gulu, Bondo in Arua and Nakasongola. These areas were suitable for grain production and could support the army’s food requirements. The responsibility of producing food for the UPDF was entrusted to its commercial arm, the National Enterprise Corporation (NEC). “A decision was taken that the army must start producing its own food and other dietary needs. This state-of-the-art sports complex is set to host matches for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), co-hosted by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. The 18-month project was completed five months ahead of schedule by Turkish firm M/S SUMMA, contracted by the government in June 2024. The $129m stadium, fully financed by Uganda's Petroleum Fund, sits on 34 acres of land and boasts a 20,000-seater capacity. The stadium's completion is expected to boost sports tourism, create jobs, and inspire young Ugandans to pursue sports and athletics. President Yoweri Museveni is set to officially open the stadium, which features modern amenities like a semi-Olympic swimming pool, indoor arena, and outdoor courts for basketball, netball, and volleyball. The facility has a hybrid turf, VVIP and VIP lounges, an indoor arena, swimming pool, Video Assistant Referee (VAR) room, multiple dressing and referee rooms, FIFA/CAF offices, media conference room, media gallery, training grounds, volleyball and basketball courts, and parking for about 1,000 cars. \u003Cstrong>CLICK \u003Ca href=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/1ff1fd8b-3528-40c1-8f13-47f944afeddf.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">HERE\u003C/a> FOR MORE ON THIS SUPPLEMENT \u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Ch3>\u003Cstrong>HOTEL OWNERS SEEK SH130B TO TRANSFORM FACILITIES\u003C/strong>\u003C/h3>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>In a bid to match the grandeur of Hoima City Stadium, hotel owners in Bunyoro are turning to the government for a sh130b Kabagambe Kaliisa, the chairperson of Bunyoro Hotel Owners Association, the stakes are high with AFCON 2027 just around the corner, and they are determined to make a lasting impression. \"This isn't just about upgrading hotels; it's about transforming Bunyoro into a premier destination,\" Kaliisa says. The plan is to expand room capacity from 160-200 to at least 900, and inject modern amenities like gyms and conference facilities. With Hoima City Stadium setting the bar high, hoteliers are feeling the pressure – and the opportunity. A proposal has already been submitted to the government via Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja, and they are hopeful for a green light. The payoff? Upgraded hotels will serve Bunyoro's booming tourism industry, showcasing gems like Murchison Falls National Park and Kibiro Hot Springs. It's a win-win: hoteliers get a boost, and Bunyoro gets a tourism facelift. \"AFCON is our moment to shine,\" Kaliisa says with a smile. \"We are not just upgrading hotels; we're investing in our region's future. Several years before that date, the “Pearl of Africa” was widely expected to be the first East African territory to achieve this goal.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>However, Tanganyika beat Uganda to the draw with a combination of factors, including its own massive African and European unity in comparison with Uganda’s obvious fragmentation.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>Clearly, in almost every outward sign, Uganda had been qualified for independence for years, but Ugandans’ inability to come together to attain their common goal delayed it until the ninth of October 1962.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>The seeds of Uganda’s disunity and lack of common national goal and purpose, were sown in 1900 within the pages of the so-called Buganda Agreement. That document stipulated that Buganda was to be the first province of Uganda, to be on the same equal status, with other provinces.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>These other provinces were to be added later as the colonialists conquered other areas. These other areas came to be known as Western Province, Eastern Province and Northern Province, making a total of four provinces of the Uganda protectorate. It was within the context of the 1900 Agreement that a clique known as the Mengo Establishment was formed.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>The clique was allotted land grants in square miles, which gave it an economic base hence helping it consolidate its power over Buganda. This clique had grabbed this power from Kabaka Mwanga II in 1888. The core of this clique consisted of Protestant elites who had triumphed at the battle of Mengo in 1892.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>Most of its members were converts to Anglican protestantism, and were allied to the British colonial power. The clique controlled the province of Buganda and influenced the events in the rest of Uganda from 1894 to 1966. It ruled Uganda for 70 years.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>The colonialists helped this clique establish a governing system whereby only its members could control the Buganda governance system. The governing system turned out to be part of the colonial policy of indirect rule, both for Buganda kingdom and, through the clique, for the whole of Uganda. In 1962, fresh from the shadows of colonial rule, just about 9% of Ugandans were part of what economists call the money economy.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>It’s a system where goods and services are exchanged for money, instead of barter. Today, that figure has shot up to 67%, a transformation that tells a powerful story of progress.\u003C/p>\u003Cp>It means millions of Ugandans are no longer working just for survival, but earning, saving, and investing in new dreams. President Yoweri Museveni once said, “The struggle we are waging is to move all our people from working for the stomach to working for the pocket.”\u003C/p>\u003Cp>That vision is now taking shape. To understand how this change happened, you have to rewind the clock. Over the past decade, UNOC has become a central player in Uganda’s oil and gas sector, signing joint operating agreements, acquiring strategic assets, taking full operatorship of the  Jinja Storage Terminal and, most recently, assuming the sole importation mandate for petroleum products. As the company embarks on its next phase, Martin Kitubi spoke with the chief executive officer, Proscovia Nabbanja, to reflect on the journey so far, the lessons learned and what lies ahead for the company.\u003C/em>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>You have been part of the 10-year journey of UNOC. Take us through the journey of the last 10 years. What have your major achievements and lessons been?\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>We established the company, set up systems and processes, and recruited staff. We are continuing to do so to manage the growing mandate. UNOC initially developed an agile strategy anchored on three pillars: Partnering strategically, investing in people, and building the business. This was the focus for the first five years and was delivered well. We are now focused on growing the business, building capabilities, and achieving operational excellence. This is important since most of the projects will be commissioned in the next few years. We aim at developing the capabilities necessary to manage these projects, with the ultimate goal of becoming independent operators in the long term. We are also building a strong culture of excellence in whatever we do. This is a differentiating factor for UNOC. Some of the key achievements include entering into joint operating agreements with the upstream oil companies to enable UNOC to manage the state’s participating interests.  \u003Cstrong>CLICK \u003Ca href=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/a6a05fa1-0719-4147-b64c-3ff2e6c68734.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">HERE\u003C/a> FOR MORE ON THIS SUPPLEMENT \u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>UNOC CHARTS PATH TO FINANCIAL INDEPENDENCE\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>\u003Cem>Last year, the Government expanded mandate of the national oil company when it entrusted it with the responsibility of being Uganda’s sole importer of petroleum products. This followed at least a year of bulk trading where Uganda National Oil Company Limited (UNOC) had supplied products to some oil marketing companies such as Stabex International Limited. Emmanuel Mugagga, UNOC’s chief financial officer spoke to New Vision on the company’s finished products arm.\u003C/em>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>Q What quantities of petroleum product is UNOC importing per month? (Breakdown on each)\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>A UNOC commenced sole importation in July last year. For the period July 2024 to June 2025, UNOC imported a total 2.676 billion litres comprising Petrol (PMS), Diesel (AGO), and Jet-A. On average, therefore, UNOC imports 240 million litres monthly and growing at an average of approximately 7-8% per annum. UNOC has come of age, and now it has been given the chance to stand on its own. Under the 2025/2026 financial year, the Government decided that UNOC can ably rely on internally generated revenue and therefore, UNOC was not capitalised to cover its operational budget. \u003Cstrong>CLICK \u003Ca href=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/a6a05fa1-0719-4147-b64c-3ff2e6c68734.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">HERE\u003C/a> FOR MORE ON THIS SUPPLEMENT \u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>OIL AND GAS GOOD FOR UGANDA’S ENERGY MIX\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp>For the next twenty years, the oil and gas sector is expected to be pivotal to Uganda’s economy. Extractives, including minerals, oil and gas, are among the four sectors earmarked to drive the tenfold economic growth strategy under the Fourth National Development Plan. The country’s nascent petroleum sector is anticipated to significantly boost the gross domestic product (GDP), create jobs, and spur industrialisation, especially in energy-intensive industries such as petrochemicals, fertilisers, and steel. With commercial oil production projected to commence in the short or medium term after the completion of key requisite infrastructure such as the East African Crude Oil Pipeline and the refinery, significant revenue inflows are expected. The sector development blueprint, Energy Policy 2023, acknowledges the strategic role that the industry will play, including providing a foundation for energy security, economic transformation, and export diversification, while emphasising value addition over raw export. Uganda is targeting an increase in installed electricity generation capacity to 52,48 megawatts from the current 2,048MW. \u003Cstrong>CLICK \u003Ca href=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/a6a05fa1-0719-4147-b64c-3ff2e6c68734.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">HERE\u003C/a> FOR MORE ON THIS SUPPLEMENT \u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>\u003Cp> \u003C/p>","TEN YEARS OF UNOC: STRATEGY, PARTNERSHIPS, AND VISION FOR INDEPENDENCE  The Uganda National Oil Company (UNOC) is celebrating 10 years of existence, a decade marked by strategic partnerships, bold investments and key milestones that have positioned Uganda closer to its first oil and greater energy security. Over the past decade, UNOC has become a central player in Uganda’s oil and gas sector, signing joint operating agreements, acquiring strategic assets, taking full operatorship of the  Jinja Storage Terminal and, most recently, assuming the sole importation mandate for petroleum products. This was the focus for the first five years and was delivered well. We are now focused on growing the business, building capabilities, and achieving operational excellence. This is important since most of the projects will be commissioned in the next few years. in Tanzania.","\u003Cp>This month, the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) project team, joined by Turkish construction firm Yapi Merkezi met local leaders from Jinja city and Jinja district as early works on the eastern route get underway. Over the past few days, the SGR team has been moving through the 12 districts along the Malaba to Kampala corridor, introducing both the contractor and the supervising consultant to local government and community leaders. Yapi Merkezi, which is handling the Malaba–Kampala section, started preliminary works in May. The Government started engaging Yapi in 2022 after they showcased their capacity to build the SGR route from Dar es Salaam to Isaka line in Tanzania. The preliminary activities by Yapi will cover mobilisation, field surveys, initial design work, identification of land that will be used temporarily and mapping of infrastructure that may need relocation. The commencement of work by the contractor follows a government decision to release funding for the first phase. In the 2025/26 fiscal year, sh2.17 trillion has been earmarked for the construction of the SGR. The secretary to the treasury Ramathan Ggoobi said: “We are prioritising things which enable these investors to make money. We are now looking at bulk transport. The construction of the railway is starting. I have provided the money to ministry of works and the contractor is on site. In next 4-5 years, we shall have the SGR.” Citi bank and a consortium of other financial institutions through export credit agency have pledged their commitments to fund the SGR. In October 2024, the Government and Yapi signed a Euro 2.7b contract for the construction of the Eastern Route. During the same time, land acquisition was nearly complete in Tororo, Butaleja, Namutumba, Luuka, Iganga, Mayuge, Jinja and Buikwe, according to information from SGR team. This, however, is only a drop in the ocean of need. The funds, provided through the UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), was aimed at enabling three UN Agencies — the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), World Food Programme (WFP) and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) to continue delivering critical services, such as food, nutrition, water, medical care and protection for refugees in their first two weeks of arrival. The response will focus on Uganda’s over-stretched transit and reception centres in Kabazana, Nyakabande and Mawanda, in Uganda’s Southwest sub-region. Uganda, already Africa’s largest refugee-hosting country, has seen a dramatic increase in new arrivals of more than 65,000 Congolese refugees from January to May this year, pushing the total number of refugees in the country to nearly 1.9 million. The sharp spike in displacement, 600% increase from the same period last year, has pushed Uganda’s reception system to a breaking point. Many refugees, mainly from DR Congo, South Sudan and Sudan, are arriving traumatised, malnourished and in urgent need of care after harrowing journeys. With food pipelines under threat, the WFP warned of serious consequences if swifter support was not implemented. “This CERF funding is a lifeline, it helps us prevent a full-blown food crisis within an already dire humanitarian emergency,” said Marcus Prior, WFP’s country director. “It enables us to deliver immediate food and nutrition support when refugees need it most — right at the point of arrival,” Prior noted. Despite restrictions, the event received widespread coverage across various media platforms. The pandemic tested the resilience of the National Resistance Movement (NRM) Government, but Uganda’s experts and multi-sectoral teams successfully contained the spread of the disease. Under President Museveni’s leadership, Uganda navigated the economic challenges posed by the pandemic, with the economy gradually recovering. The Government implemented measures to mitigate its impact, including vaccine development. Local scientists, led by Prof. Patrick Ogwang, developed Covidex, a supportive treatment for COVID-19. President Museveni highlighted Uganda’s economic progress, citing an annual growth rate of 6.2% over 35 years. He projected further growth with the activation of the oil sector, aiming for 9–10% growth in the initial years of oil production. Despite this progress, President Museveni emphasised the need for faster growth rates, leveraging Uganda’s improved literacy rate. The country has transformed from a nation of shortages in 1986 to one of surpluses today, with significant production in maize, milk, bananas, beef, sugar, cement, steel bars, and textiles. The NRM government has prioritised five key areas: wealth creation, education and health, justice and equity, protection of life and property and economic integration. Under President Museveni’s leadership, Uganda has contributed to regional peace and security, hosting refugees and supporting peace efforts in neighbouring countries. The Uganda People’s Defence Force has played a vital role in various regional peacekeeping missions. President Museveni has pledged to tackle corruption, with a focus on industrialisation and reducing production costs. The NRM government is working towards integrating Uganda into the African Free Trade Area and the East African Confederation. He encouraged believers to remain steadfast in their faith while facing the challenges of modern life and to continue promoting peace, unity and love within their communities.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The annual commemoration honours the Uganda Martyrs, a group of 22 Catholic and 23 Anglican converts who were executed during the reign of Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda. The young men were killed after refusing to renounce Christianity and rejecting demands that conflicted with their religious beliefs.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Their persecution began in 1885 as Christianity continued to spread within the Buganda Kingdom. Concerned by the growing influence of the new faith among members of his royal court, Kabaka Mwanga II launched a campaign against Christian converts.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Among the first Anglican martyrs to be killed were Kakumba Makko, Yusuf Rugarama and Nuwa Sserwanga, who were executed in January 1885. The persecution intensified in 1886 when several converts faced torture, mutilation, beheading and execution for refusing to abandon their faith.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>One of the most notable figures among the martyrs was Charles Lwanga, who emerged as a leader of the Christian pages. He encouraged fellow believers to remain faithful despite the threat of death. His courage and leadership continue to inspire Christians around the world.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The most remembered event in the history of the Uganda Martyrs occurred on June 3, 1886, when a large group of converts was marched to Namugongo and burnt alive. Among those executed was Kizito, the youngest of the martyrs, whose unwavering faith has become a symbol of courage for young Christians.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Several Catholic martyrs, including Lukka Baanabakintu, James Buuzabalyawo, Gyaviira Musoke, Ambrosius Kibuuka, Anatoli Kiriggwajjo, Mukasa Kiriwawanvu, Achileo Kiwanuka, Adolphus Mukasa Ludigo, Mugagga Lubowa, Bruno Sserunkuuma and Mbaga Tuzinde, died alongside their companions at Namugongo.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The Anglican martyrs who perished at Namugongo included Nuwa Walukagga, Alexander Kadoko, Frederick Kizza, Robert Munyagabyangu, Danieri Nakabandwa, Kiwanuka Giyaza, Mukasa Lwakisiga, Mubi Azaalwa, Kwabafu, Kifamunnyanja and Muwanga Njigiya. Other martyrs were speared, beheaded or subjected to brutal punishment in different parts of Buganda.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Although the executions were intended to suppress Christianity, they instead strengthened the faith and accelerated its spread throughout Uganda. The courage displayed by the martyrs inspired many people to embrace Christianity, contributing to the growth of the Church across the country.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Today, Namugongo remains one of Africa’s most important Christian pilgrimage destinations, attracting millions of believers every year. The shrine stands as a symbol of faith, sacrifice, perseverance and devotion.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As Christians marked this year’s Uganda Martyrs Day under the shadow of an Ebola outbreak, church leaders emphasised that the martyrs’ legacy remains relevant. On October 18, 1964, at St Peter’s Basilica, Pope Paul VI canonised 22 Catholic martyrs from Uganda.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Kasujja explained that St Charles Lwanga was burnt at the site where the Catholic shrine now stands, while other martyrs continued to Nakiyanja-Namugongo, where they were executed alongside 13 Anglican martyrs.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He said their sacrifice remains a powerful example of ecumenical witness and solidarity in the Christian faith.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The prelate noted that the martyrs encouraged one another in faith and Christian values even as they shed their blood for Christ, an example that continues to inspire believers today.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Shrine rector\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>Fr Lubega said Namugongo is an international pilgrimage destination that normally hosts millions of people from countries across Africa, Asia and Europe.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Although this year's celebrations were scaled down following restrictions linked to the Ebola outbreak, he welcomed the opportunity for Christians to gather and pray.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He said: “We are happy that President Yoweri Museveni didn’t refuse us to gather and pray.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Fr Lubega added that “as they asked all Christians to commemorate the day from their respective parishes and Dioceses, we urged all the parishioners to follow the SOPs we have provided, we have the medical workers on the site who are helping us measure the temperature to everyone, sanitisers and fumigate the shrine every time after masses.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“To cater to this, we have put several Masses to avoid people being squeezed in the Shrine, and we asked them to keep their distance.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">About Uganda Martyrs\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>Uganda Martyrs Day is a national public holiday celebrated annually on June 3. It commemorates the 45 Christian converts, comprising 22 Catholics and 23 Anglicans, who were executed by Kabaka Mwanga II between 1885 and 1887.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The 22 Catholic martyrs were beatified on June 6, 1920, by Pope Benedict XV and canonised on October 18, 1964, by Pope Paul VI.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Apart from the 22 martyrs, Christians also commemorate Blessed Daudi Okello and Jildo Irwa, catechists in northern Uganda who were killed at Paimol in 1915.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For the Catholic Church, Martyrs Day celebrations are organised on a rotational basis among the country's four ecclesiastical provinces.","______________The Emeritus Apostolic Nuncio to Belgium, Archbishop Augustine Kasujja, has challenged Uganda's young people to emulate the courage, discipline and faith of the Uganda Martyrs by rejecting immorality, corruption, laziness and other vices that continue to undermine society.Speaking during Holy Mass at the Catholic Shrine Martyrs Basilica in Namugongo, Wakiso district, on Wednesday (June 3), Kasujja said the witness of the Uganda Martyrs remains relevant today, particularly for young people navigating growing social and moral challenges.He said: “My dear brothers and sisters, especially young of Ugandans, our Martyrs who were majority young like you, they invite us today follow in their footsteps, to influence and change the issue the of our society and resist the temptation of today; corruption, morality, laziness, land grabbing, injustice enrichments and family conflicts and felinities, brethren nothing possible to resist if we create a new spiritual prayer with God.Archbishop Kasujja made the remarks while preaching during Holy Mass at the Catholic Shrine Martyrs Basilica in Namugongo, where this year's Martyrs Day prayers were held in place of the traditional open-air celebrations.He was assisted by 13 priests from different parishes, including the secretary of the Apostolic Nunciature to Uganda, Fr Georges Kwami Kouwonou, who represented Pope Leo XIV on behalf of the Papal Nuncio. Others included Fr George, the shrine rector, Fr Vincent Lubega, head of the White Fathers in Uganda, and Fr Richard Nyombi.The celebrations were also attended by a group of 25 choir members from Germany who had travelled to join this year's host diocese, Kasese. However, because of the Ebola outbreak, they were unable to participate as originally planned.Strict health measures were observed at Namugongo, with all worshippers screened and having their temperatures checked before entering the shrine to prevent the spread of Ebola.Furthermore, the prelate said that the “Pope Paul VI statement on the canonisation continued challenging all Christians and non-Christians in Uganda to follow in the ecumenical footsteps of our poor fathers in faith. When Pope Paul VI travelled later in Uganda and visited both shrines (Catholics and Anglicans) on August 2, 1969, he said that your Martyrs teach us just who the true Christians should be, especially young African Christians. They were courageous, strong and firm in faith. We pray that we acquire the advice of the Pope.”The Archbishop also reminded worshippers at the Namugongo Basilica of remarks made by Pope Paul VI during the canonisation of the Uganda Martyrs. On October 18, 1964, at St Peter’s Basilica, Pope Paul VI canonised 22 Catholic martyrs from Uganda.Kasujja explained that St Charles Lwanga was burnt at the site where the Catholic shrine now stands, while other martyrs continued to Nakiyanja-Namugongo, where they were executed alongside 13 Anglican martyrs.He said their sacrifice remains a powerful example of ecumenical witness and solidarity in the Christian faith.The prelate noted that the martyrs encouraged one another in faith and Christian values even as they shed their blood for Christ, an example that continues to inspire believers today.Shrine rectorFr Lubega said Namugongo is an international pilgrimage destination that normally hosts millions of people from countries across Africa, Asia and Europe.Although this year's celebrations were scaled down following restrictions linked to the Ebola outbreak, he welcomed the opportunity for Christians to gather and pray.He said: “We are happy that President Yoweri Museveni didn’t refuse us to gather and pray.”Fr Lubega added that “as they asked all Christians to commemorate the day from their respective parishes and Dioceses, we urged all the parishioners to follow the SOPs we have provided, we have the medical workers on the site who are helping us measure the temperature to everyone, sanitisers and fumigate the shrine every time after masses.“To cater to this, we have put several Masses to avoid people being squeezed in the Shrine, and we asked them to keep their distance.”About Uganda MartyrsUganda Martyrs Day is a national public holiday celebrated annually on June 3. 13:57:00","Anglican Church holds virtual Uganda Martyrs Day prayers","anglican-church-holds-virtual-uganda-martyrs","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">KAMPALA - \u003Cstrong>A number of religious leaders and selected dignitaries, including government officials, attended Martyrs Day virtual prayers presided over by the Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba, at the Anglican Shrine in Namugongo.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The Church encouraged faithful to join the service through television, radio and online platforms following the Government’s decision to suspend physical pilgrimages due to the Ebola outbreak.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Among the senior government officials in attendance were former Prime Minister Amama Mbabazi and his wife, State Minister for Elderly Affairs-designate Jackline Mbabazi, Minister of Public Service designate Gen Katumba Wamala, outgoing Energy Minister Ruth Nankabirwa, and State Minister for Trade David Bahati.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The service also attracted prominent religious leaders, including Rt Rev. Prof Alfred Olwa, Bishop of Lango Diocese and chairman of the Uganda Joint Christian Council; Rt Rev. Jackson Frederick Baalwa, Episcopal Bishop of Kampala; Rt Rev. Jackson Matovu, Bishop Emeritus of Central Buganda Diocese and chairman of the Uganda Martyrs Museum; as well as Rev. Canon Prof Olivia Nassaka Banja, Vice Chancellor of Ndejje University and Mama Bishop of Namirembe.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Others in attendance included Canon Prof. Aaron Mushengyezi, vice chancellor of Uganda Christian University, and Prof. Kayiwa Ingo, the university’s deputy vice chancellor.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/1172fb97-ab8f-4375-80d9-2b7c6fc07a51.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cbr>Leadership praises organisers and government support\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Speaking while welcoming guests at Namugongo, Namirembe Diocese Bishop Moses Banja commended Uganda Christian University for successfully organising this year’s virtual Martyrs Day celebrations and for undertaking significant improvements at the Anglican Shrine.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"I want to appreciate, in a special way, Uganda Christian University and its leadership for organising this year's Martyrs' Celebration,\" Banja said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He noted that the institution had transformed the appearance of the shrine through several infrastructure projects.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"We have seen a lot has taken place in this place. Our seminary has changed its face, and many, many things that you have done the walkways, the washrooms, the modern facilities in this place, and even painting our buildings,\" he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Thank God for you who have come, that you are seeing what the Lord has done through the organising university,” he added.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Bishop Banja also thanked President Yoweri Museveni and the Government for supporting the Church of Uganda to hold the celebrations despite the public health challenges facing the country.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Allow me also to thank His Excellency the President of the Republic of Uganda for allowing us to celebrate this year's Martyrs' Celebration virtually, and all the support that the government has given us to see what we see today. We praise God for that,\" he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/ef06d042-42bf-4193-aed4-4711981f1657.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cbr>Call for permanent church structure\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The Bishop used the occasion to appeal for support towards the construction of a permanent church for Namugongo Martyrs Archdeaconry, noting that worshippers have endured difficult conditions for years.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"I want to inform Your Grace and all those who have come to celebrate this year's Martyrs' Celebration that our Christians here in Namugongo have suffered a lot,\" he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Banja, Christians have been holding services in a temporary tent known as the Tabernacle for more than five years, despite the area being elevated to an archdeaconry status.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"They have been having their services in a tent they call it Tabernacle over there. For over five years or so, they have been having their services there. This place was raised to the level of an archdeaconry, but they do not have a church, a proper church, to worship God,” Banja said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He revealed that church authorities had already approved plans for the construction of the Namugongo Martyrs Archdeaconry Church and that fundraising efforts had begun.\u003Cbr>\"Over that site, where you see some construction ongoing, that is where we are going to construct the Namugongo Martyrs Archdeaconry Church,\" he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/b0e61e0b-00b6-4ad9-82a2-0694d2a28120.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cbr>Background on Uganda Martyrs Day\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>Uganda Martyrs Day, observed annually on June 3, is one of the country’s most significant religious events, drawing millions of pilgrims from Uganda and beyond to honour the faith and sacrifice of the Uganda Martyrs.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The day commemorates 45 young Christian converts who were executed between 1885 and 1887 on the orders of Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda for refusing to renounce their faith. The martyrs included both Catholics and Anglicans who remained steadfast in their beliefs despite persecution and death.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The main celebrations are held at Namugongo, where many of the martyrs were killed. Thousands of pilgrims travel long distances on foot from different parts of Uganda and neighbouring countries to take part in prayers, Masses and other religious activities.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Over the years, Uganda Martyrs Day has grown into a major spiritual and cultural event promoting faith, unity, courage and perseverance. The martyrs are remembered as symbols of conviction, integrity and sacrifice, inspiring generations of Christians.","KAMPALA - A number of religious leaders and selected dignitaries, including government officials, attended Martyrs Day virtual prayers presided over by the Archbishop of the Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba, at the Anglican Shrine in Namugongo.The Church encouraged faithful to join the service through television, radio and online platforms following the Government’s decision to suspend physical pilgrimages due to the Ebola outbreak.Among the senior government officials in attendance were former Prime Minister Amama Mbabazi and his wife, State Minister for Elderly Affairs-designate Jackline Mbabazi, Minister of Public Service designate Gen Katumba Wamala, outgoing Energy Minister Ruth Nankabirwa, and State Minister for Trade David Bahati.The service also attracted prominent religious leaders, including Rt Rev. Prof Alfred Olwa, Bishop of Lango Diocese and chairman of the Uganda Joint Christian Council; Rt Rev. Jackson Frederick Baalwa, Episcopal Bishop of Kampala; Rt Rev. Jackson Matovu, Bishop Emeritus of Central Buganda Diocese and chairman of the Uganda Martyrs Museum; as well as Rev. Canon Prof Olivia Nassaka Banja, Vice Chancellor of Ndejje University and Mama Bishop of Namirembe.Others in attendance included Canon Prof. Aaron Mushengyezi, vice chancellor of Uganda Christian University, and Prof. Kayiwa Ingo, the university’s deputy vice chancellor.Leadership praises organisers and government supportSpeaking while welcoming guests at Namugongo, Namirembe Diocese Bishop Moses Banja commended Uganda Christian University for successfully organising this year’s virtual Martyrs Day celebrations and for undertaking significant improvements at the Anglican Shrine.\"I want to appreciate, in a special way, Uganda Christian University and its leadership for organising this year's Martyrs' Celebration,\" Banja said.He noted that the institution had transformed the appearance of the shrine through several infrastructure projects.\"We have seen a lot has taken place in this place. Our seminary has changed its face, and many, many things that you have done the walkways, the washrooms, the modern facilities in this place, and even painting our buildings,\" he said.\"Thank God for you who have come, that you are seeing what the Lord has done through the organising university,” he added.Bishop Banja also thanked President Yoweri Museveni and the Government for supporting the Church of Uganda to hold the celebrations despite the public health challenges facing the country.\"Allow me also to thank His Excellency the President of the Republic of Uganda for allowing us to celebrate this year's Martyrs' Celebration virtually, and all the support that the government has given us to see what we see today. We praise God for that,\" he said.Call for permanent church structureThe Bishop used the occasion to appeal for support towards the construction of a permanent church for Namugongo Martyrs Archdeaconry, noting that worshippers have endured difficult conditions for years.\"I want to inform Your Grace and all those who have come to celebrate this year's Martyrs' Celebration that our Christians here in Namugongo have suffered a lot,\" he said.According to Banja, Christians have been holding services in a temporary tent known as the Tabernacle for more than five years, despite the area being elevated to an archdeaconry status.\"They have been having their services in a tent they call it Tabernacle over there. For over five years or so, they have been having their services there. This place was raised to the level of an archdeaconry, but they do not have a church, a proper church, to worship God,” Banja said.He revealed that church authorities had already approved plans for the construction of the Namugongo Martyrs Archdeaconry Church and that fundraising efforts had begun.\"Over that site, where you see some construction ongoing, that is where we are going to construct the Namugongo Martyrs Archdeaconry Church,\" he said.Background on Uganda Martyrs DayUganda Martyrs Day, observed annually on June 3, is one of the country’s most significant religious events, drawing millions of pilgrims from Uganda and beyond to honour the faith and sacrifice of the Uganda Martyrs.The day commemorates 45 young Christian converts who were executed between 1885 and 1887 on the orders of Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda for refusing to renounce their faith. disease.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>The government recently directed that Martyrs Day celebrations be held at parish level instead of attracting the massive congregations traditionally Dr Stephen Samuel Kaziimba Mugalu, assigned Uganda Christian University (UCU) to continue organising this year’s scientific celebrations and also prepare to coordinate next year’s Uganda Martyrs’ Day celebrations. On Wednesday, the archbishop visited the Uganda Martyrs’ Anglican Site at Namugongo to assess the readiness of UCU to host this year’s commemorations.The Mukono-based university was mandated by the House of Bishops to organise this year’s celebrations on behalf of Church of Uganda.Since assuming this responsibility, the university has undertaken significant improvements at the site in several key areas, including security and safety, beautification, branding, and improving sanitation and water supply.Among the notable developments are the construction and renovation of modern toilet facilities, establishment of walkways, restoration of the green environment, reconstruction of sections of the collapsed perimeter wall to enhance security, drilling and construction of a water solar powered supply system, renovation of several buildings at the site and general clean-up of the site.The initial expectation was that the site would welcome thousands of pilgrims, as has been the case in previous years.However, the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo has necessitated a change of plans. Our new home.” House of Jazz first came to our attention in 2023, when they hosted the Kampala Jazz Orchestra and Kenyan musician Bien-Aime Baraza, formerly of the group Sauti Sol, at the Latitude 0 hotel in Makindye.  A year later, they paired the orchestra with singer Maurice Kirya in the Orchestra in the City at the Uganda Golf Club green. In both cases, it was a combination of fine dining and music, especially jazz. Then they went quiet. That was because they were cooking, said Jackie Karuletwa Kakiza, one of the directors. And what they cooked was served on Saturday at their home on Nviri Lane, Kololo. And it was their friends on the guest list. Notably missing were the usual Kampala celebrities that seem to be at every function, and the only musicians I saw were Solome Basuuta (who is set to perform at the official opening at the end of the month) and Isaiah Katumwa. Even the media was missing. What was not missing was the music, obviously. And good food. Herbert Ssesamba on acoustic guitar and David Olara on saxophone welcomed the guests, before Essie Ariho took over the main performing duties.   After a couple of jazz songs (including Ella Fitzgerald’s evergreen Summertime), which she did reasonably well, it was on to pop. K!mera did his thing and got everyone dancing, and Valentino wound up the night with creative dancing. The three women behind the House of Jazz (Mawadri, Candy Wekesa Okoboi and Karuletwa) promised to make it a centre of discovering Ugandan talent. What was loudly missing was actual jazz, but the three ladies promised that jazz in Uganda had finally found a home, and for us to watch this space. (Photo by Nicholas Oneal \u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>The play’s return to the stage gave many theatre lovers another chance to experience a production that has become one of Uganda’s standout theatrical works.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The play is not a monologue of a show but a dialogue with the audience who are craftily called in to play alongside the actor.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Set at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic when strict curfews were set, and we did not know how to go about everything, the audience meets Kabibi, a dishevelled and young fashionable ‘slay queen’ copywriter who turns up at the bus stop with her belongings on Kampala streets after falling out with her roommate Shishi.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She is stranded and does not know where to go next. Amidst the chaos of rising death tolls announced on Zed FM by anchor Lady TK (voiced by actress Gloria Nambozo) and Taxi touts, Boda Boda hoots, ambulance/police sirens on the street, Kabibi just sat on a bench. It was an image many could instantly recognise.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>From there, the story unfolded as Kabibi is forced into an emotional and psychological unravelling of her fractured childhood and past events that led to her present. style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">The Triplets Ghetto Kids returned home to a heroes' welcome on Monday, August 03, 2026, after making history on the global stage with a groundbreaking performance at the FIFA World Cup final halftime show.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The group landed at Entebbe International Airport at around 10:00 a.m. to jubilant scenes as fellow dancers, fans, friends and well-wishers gathered to receive them.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/007f25e0-5312-404d-b51c-7efcaa5615e7.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>Waving Ugandan flags and chanting their names, supporters celebrated the young dancers' remarkable achievement of representing the country before millions of viewers worldwide.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The excitement did not end at the airport, as the convoy made its way from Entebbe to Nakivubo Hamz Stadium in Kampala, where crowds lined sections of the road to catch a glimpse of the dancers.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Eight Ugandan children were selected to perform alongside global music stars Shakira and Burna Boy during the first-ever FIFA World Cup final halftime show on July 19, 2026. Spain beat Argentina 1-0 to lift the coveted trophy.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/deec2dfd-bf9c-4a0e-b50d-bb308cf2e75e.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>Speaking at the press conference, the group's caretaker, Dauda Kavuma, described the journey as challenging but worthwhile. price","museveni-calls-for-preservation-of-cultural-t","\u003Cp>__________________\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni has urged the Banyankole community to preserve the cultural values of the traditional Okuhingira ceremony by discouraging excessive bride price demands and extravagant weddings, warning that the growing commercialisation of marriage is discouraging many young people from starting families.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>The President made the remarks on Saturday 1\u003Csup>st\u003C/sup> Robert Kato","The transition from a transitional deacon to a priest is the culmination of years of spiritual, academic, and pastoral formation. This sacred journey shifts a man from a minister of service into the ministerial priesthood, granting him the lifelong authority to consecrate the Eucharist. The day of ordination is a profoundly moving experience. For most Catholic ordinands, the rite unfolds through several deeply symbolic steps.An ordained priest is a religious leader who has received sacred authority through a formal rite called Holy Orders. They act as ministers of holy sacraments, teachers of faith, and spiritual leaders for their local church.On Saturday (August 1), four Catholic Dioceses ordained 42 deacons to the priesthood and 32 seminarians to the diaconate.The bishops ordained the priests and deacons in procedures, including making promises of obedience to their bishops and their successors, along with a commitment to celibacy and the lifelong prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.Those ordained included two Brothers of Bannakalooli congregation in Kiteredde in Kyotera District, under Masaka Diocese.The four Catholic Dioceses received 42 new priests: Kiyinda-Mityana (7), Arua (9), Masaka (20) and Fort-Portal (6).
