20:44:22","Controversy as court stops NEMA, KCCA from closing noisy city bar","controversy-as-court-stops-nema-kcca-from-clo","\u003Cp>______________\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">Controversy surrounds circumstances under which court issued an injunction stopping city authorities from taking action against a bar located in the city suburbs of Kololo, which emits noise above permissible levels.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The court order signed by High Court Civil Division Registrar Simon Kintu Zirintusa was secured by the owners of Aurous Restaurant and Fine Dining bar against Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA) and the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA).\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>This was after Kololo residents repeatedly petitioned KCCA and NEMA over noise pollution by Aurous Bar, prompting KCCA to write to the bar owners asking them to soundproof the bar or risk closure and confiscation of their equipment over noise pollution.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>It has also emerged that some residents have since sued the management of Aurous Bar, located on Plot 11 Roscoe Road, for consistently emitting noise beyond the legally accepted levels, especially during nighttime.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The National Environment (Noise Standards and Control) Regulations, 2003 (under sections 28 and 107 of the National Environment Act Cap 153), clearly spell out the permissible noise levels by entertainment places.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For places or establishments of entertainment in residential areas, the permissible noise levels are 60 decibels during day (6:00 am to 10:00 pm) and 40 decibels at night (10:00 pm to 6:00 am).\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>If the places or establishments of entertainment are in commercial areas, the permissible noise levels are 75 decibels during day and 50 decibels at night. If such a place is in an industrial area, the permissible noise levels are 85 decibels during day and 65 decibels at night.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The generally accepted noise levels in residential buildings are 50 decibels during day and 35 decibels at night, while in mixed residential (with some commercial and entertainment), the day noise limits are 55 decibels and night limits stand at 35 decibels.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Section 17(1) of the regulations states: “An environmental inspector, the executive director, or a member of a local council may seize, impound, or confiscate any property, tool, machinery, or other instrument, which is likely to cause or has caused the emission of noise if, in his or her opinion, the confiscation would cause tranquility in the area.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>However, \u003Cem>New Vision\u003C/em> has learnt that instead of complying with the NEMA and KCCA requirements to contain noise, the Aurous bar management went to court and secured an injunction stopping the two entities from closing their business and confiscating their equipment.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The injunction, which was first issued on August 15, 2025, and is still in force to date, restrains KCCA, NEMA and their agents \"from closing, interfering with the applicant’s business, and from confiscating its tools of trade until the hearing and final determination of the main suit.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The injunction followed a letter from KCCA executive director Sharifah Buzeki in which she revealed that besides emitting noise, Aurous bar was also operating without a development permit.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Following routine inspections and neighbourly complaints received regarding noise nuisance resulting from your operations, an enforcement notice was issued to you on November 14, 2024, requiring you to, among other things, halt operations, remove all temporary structures, and obtain change of use,” Buzeki wrote on May 21, 2025.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>It emerged that the building in which Aurous Bar is operating has a residential permit and not a commercial permit.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Documents show that the National Planning Authority last year advised KCCA to ensure that the proprietors apply for change of use as required under the law – from residential to commercial permit.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As a result, KCCA gave the building owner and proprietors of Aurous Bar 14 days to comply. KCCA also asked them to remove the illegal structures erected or have them removed by the council at their cost.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The letter was sent to the owner of Aurous Bar (Martin Kasenge) and also copied to Zhang Zhengguo, the proprietor of the building that houses the bar.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In response, however, the bar management went to court and secured an order stopping KCCA and NEMA from interfering with their business.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>This has incensed residents, who now have to bear with the noise from the bar until the matter is resolved by court.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>KCCA, NEMA comment\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>KCCA spokesperson Daniel Muhumuza Nuweabine confirmed that the proprietor of Aurous Bar successfully sought a court order halting the enforcement of action against their business.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Nuweabine said Aurous Bar had installed soundproofing to contain noise. However, documents signed by inspectors, who visited the bar last Saturday (July 4), found it emitting noise beyond the permissible levels.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The inspection report shows that whereas the bar was expected to emit noise not exceeding 35 decibels at night, it was found emitting noise measuring between 62 and 64 decibels at the time of inspection.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Naome Karekaho, NEMA's Corporate Public Relations Officer, said although many licensed bars in Kampala violate environmental laws and guidelines, each case is handled on its own merits.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"I have not yet received feedback from our inspectors, but once a matter is before court, no further action can be taken because it would be regarded as sub judice,\" she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Karekaho stressed that NEMA's enforcement decisions are guided strictly by the law.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Lawyers weigh in\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Solomon Ssebbowa, a lawyer at Katende and Company Advocates, said the directives issued by KCCA and NEMA are administrative decisions exercised under their statutory mandates.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He explained that any person aggrieved by such decisions has the right to seek judicial review before the High Court and apply for appropriate remedies, including an injunction.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"They can obtain an injunction to stop the implementation of the administrative decision,\" Ssebbowa said, adding that once granted, the injunction remains in force until the court determines the case or sets it aside.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Constitutional lawyer Peter Walubiri also noted that courts have powers to suspend enforcement decisions made by regulatory agencies through injunctions. However, he noted that KCCA and NEMA retain the legal authority to suspend or close businesses found to be generating excessive noise.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Ambrose Byaruhanga, the chairperson of Kololo, said he had not yet received official complaints from locals. That if we pray, we’ll get a man of God. If we campaign, we’ll get a half-cooked product of the devil. So we better pray that God will raise a man to take over after our outgoing Archbishop, our dear brother Dr. Stephen Kaziimba,” said Orombi on Friday.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He was addressing a huge gathering at Uganda Christian University’s (UCU) 27th graduation ceremony held on the university’s main campus in Mukono.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Orombi’s remarks came as the university celebrated the achievements of 1,274 graduates, including two who earned Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) degrees and 102 who attained first-class honours.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In a wide-ranging address filled with gratitude and spiritual counsel, Orombi, who was the Chief Guest, reflected warmly on his own connection to UCU, noting that his life and ministry were deeply intertwined with the institution when he studied there between 1975 and 1978. \u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He commended the university for maintaining one of the most beautiful and well-kept campuses on the African continent.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“I believe Uganda Christian University is the most beautiful, cleanest, adorable, attractive university in Africa,” he declared. style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Health officials in Bushenyi district have called on employers to establish breastfeeding-friendly workplaces, saying the absence of breastfeeding corners is preventing many working mothers from exclusively breastfeeding their babies during the first six months of life.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>The appeal comes as Uganda joins the rest of the world in commemorating World Breastfeeding Week, observed annually from August 1 to 7 to raise awareness about the importance of breastfeeding and mobilise support for mothers, babies, families and communities.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Working mothers face challenges\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Speaking to \u003Cem>New Vision\u003C/em>, Bushenyi district nutrition focal person Nancy Nyamweya said many mothers return to work before their babies are six months old, making it difficult to follow the Ministry of Health's recommendation on exclusive breastfeeding.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Many mothers are willing to exclusively breastfeed their babies, but the challenge is that most workplaces do not have breastfeeding corners. Without such facilities, mothers are forced to interrupt breastfeeding, which affects both the mother and the baby,\" Nyamweya said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She said breastfeeding-friendly workplaces would enable mothers to continue breastfeeding even after resuming work, helping to improve children's health and nutrition.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Importance of exclusive breastfeeding\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Nyamweya urged mothers to exclusively breastfeed their babies for the first six months of life, explaining that breast milk provides all the nutrients, energy and antibodies an infant needs during that period.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is one of the most effective ways of ensuring children grow healthy. After six months, mothers should introduce safe and nutritious complementary foods while continuing to breastfeed until the child reaches two years or beyond,\" she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She added that breastfeeding protects babies against common childhood illnesses, strengthens their immunity, promotes healthy growth and development, and reduces the risk of malnutrition.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Employers urged to support mothers\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Nyamweya appealed to employers in both the public and private sectors to establish breastfeeding corners and adopt policies that support nursing mothers.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Providing breastfeeding corners is not a luxury. It is an investment in the health and future of our children.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Employers should create a supportive environment that enables mothers to breastfeed or express breast milk during working hours,\" she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Mothers speak out\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Aheebwa Mary, a teacher at Kajunju Primary School in Bushenyi district and the mother of a four-month-old baby, said many working mothers struggle to exclusively breastfeed because of their work schedules.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"We leave our babies at home early in the morning and return late in the evening. This makes exclusive breastfeeding difficult. I appeal to employers to create breastfeeding-friendly workplaces and give nursing mothers enough time to breastfeed because it is important for the child's growth and development,\" she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She added that greater support from employers would enable mothers to continue breastfeeding while fulfilling their responsibilities at work.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Global campaign\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>World Breastfeeding Week is commemorated every year from August 1 to 7 by governments, health institutions and communities worldwide to promote breastfeeding and improve maternal and child health.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organisation, infants 18:56:58","Can breastfeeding reduce thumb sucking?","can-breastfeeding-reduce-thumb-sucking","\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>________________   \u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Breastfeeding does far more than satisfy a baby's hunger. Child health experts say it also provides comfort, strengthens emotional bonding and may reduce the likelihood of prolonged thumb sucking by meeting a child's need for both nourishment and security.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">Thumb sucking is a normal part of infancy, with most babies naturally discovering their fingers within the first few months of life. While the behaviour is considered a healthy developmental reflex during early childhood, experts say the way a baby is fed can influence how long the habit lasts.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">According to Dr Musa Katende, Managing Director of M Dental Care in Kampala, regular breastfeeding helps meet both a baby's physical and emotional needs, reducing the desire to seek additional comfort through thumb sucking.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">\"The more you feed them, the less urge for thumb sucking,\" he says.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">His observation reflects what paediatric specialists say about the important role breastfeeding plays in a child's emotional development. Feeding time is not simply about providing nutrition. It is also a period of close physical contact, warmth and reassurance that helps babies feel safe and secure.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">Developmental paediatrician Dr Caroline Nerima says breastfeeding offers benefits that extend well beyond nourishment. It strengthens the emotional bond between mother and child while helping babies develop a sense of security during the earliest stages of life.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">Children who breastfeed for only a short time, she explains, may continue thumb sucking for longer because they are more likely to seek comfort through other means.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">\"Breastfeeding offers more than nourishment,\" Nerima explains. \"It strengthens emotional security and bonding, making children less likely to seek comfort elsewhere.\"\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">This does not mean that every child who is breastfed will never suck their thumb, nor does it suggest that children who were not breastfed will automatically develop prolonged thumb-sucking habits. Instead, experts say breastfeeding is one of several factors that can influence how children learn to comfort themselves as they grow.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">Thumb sucking itself begins as a completely normal developmental behaviour. Babies are born with a natural sucking reflex that helps them feed and survive. Without accurate diagnosis, there is no timely treatment, and without early detection, lives are unnecessarily lost,” he explained.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">He added that the laboratory on wheels will extend quality diagnostic services to villages, islands and underserved communities, enabling thousands of Ugandans to know their health status earlier and begin treatment before illnesses become severe.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">Meanwhile, Deepak Sharma, a representative of the Indo-Africa Charitable Society, said the project was inspired by the organisation's chairman, Vasant Lakhani, who was born in Jinja and has supported medical outreach programmes in Uganda for nearly two decades.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">According to Sharma, previous medical camps faced major challenges because blood samples had to be transported to hospitals for testing, delaying diagnosis and treatment.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">“This laboratory allows us to conduct most blood tests right at the medical camp. Now we can run laboratory tests on-site, get results quickly and begin managing patients without unnecessary delays,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">The Indo-Africa Charitable Society, a charitable organisation registered in Vancouver, Canada, has worked in Uganda for nearly 20 years, supporting free medical camps, humanitarian initiatives, borehole construction and specialised treatment for patients requiring cardiac surgery.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">If successfully deployed, the mobile laboratory could reduce \u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">delays in diagnosis\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\"> for thousands of people in remote communities, allowing patients to begin treatment earlier and improving outcomes for diseases that are often detected too late.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan data-preserver-spaces=\"true\">Health experts say timely diagnosis is key to reducing preventable deaths from both infectious and non-communicable diseases, particularly in communities where many patients seek treatment only after diseases have advanced.\u003C/span>\u003C/p>","   ________________    Thousands of residents in underserved communities are expected to benefit from faster and more accessible diagnostic services after Buganda Kingdom received a sh200 million mobile medical laboratory designed to conduct on-site testing during medical outreach programmes.For many residents in remote parts of Buganda, a simple blood test can mean travelling long distances and waiting days for results, allowing treatable diseases to worsen. That could soon change.The fully equipped mobile medical laboratory, donated by the Indo-Africa Charitable Society, was officially handed over on July 31, 2026, during a ceremony attended by Buganda Katikkiro Charles Peter Mayiga, India's High Commissioner to Uganda Anantha S.R. Iyer, government officials, development partners, religious leaders and health professionals.Unlike conventional outreach programmes that focus mainly on treatment, the mobile laboratory will enable healthcare teams to conduct blood tests and other diagnostic procedures on-site during medical camps, allowing patients to receive results and referrals without travelling long distances.Speaking after receiving the donation, Katikkiro Charles Peter Mayiga said the facility will strengthen the kingdom's efforts to improve people's health by extending services to communities that are often left behind.“Our vision is to place the people of the kingdom at the centre of social and economic development, but that is not realisable if people are not in good health,” he said. He noted that the laboratory complements Buganda Kingdom's existing mobile hospital by filling a major gap in disease diagnosis.“Diagnosis is very important. The people most affected are those in far-off areas where health centres are not easily accessible.”“This mobile laboratory will go to those communities to take care of the health of the ordinary person,” he elaborated.Mayiga said the kingdom will rely on its network of chiefs across the 18 counties to identify the communities most in need and coordinate outreach programmes.The donation comes as Buganda commemorates the 33rd Coronation Anniversary of Kabaka Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II, with the donor describing the laboratory as a tribute to the King's legacy of promoting health, education and community development.Representation of hopeSpeaking on behalf of the Indo-Africa Charitable Society, coordinator Simon Mugerwa described the laboratory as more than a vehicle, saying it represents \"hope, access and dignity\" for communities that have long struggled to obtain reliable diagnostic services.The organisation developed the mobile laboratory after years of witnessing patients fail to receive timely diagnoses during medical outreach programmes.Mugerwa said many preventable deaths occur because people cannot access laboratory services early enough to detect diseases such as malaria, HIV, diabetes, hypertension, sickle cell disease and other infectious and non-communicable illnesses.“Before treatment comes diagnosis. Without accurate diagnosis, there is no timely treatment, and without early detection, lives are unnecessarily lost,” he explained.He added that the laboratory on wheels will extend quality diagnostic services to villages, islands and underserved communities, enabling thousands of Ugandans to know their health status earlier and begin treatment before illnesses become severe.Meanwhile, Deepak Sharma, a representative of the Indo-Africa Charitable Society, said the project was inspired by the organisation's chairman, Vasant Lakhani, who was born in Jinja and has supported medical outreach programmes in Uganda for nearly two decades.According to Sharma, previous medical camps faced major challenges because blood samples had to be transported to hospitals for testing, delaying diagnosis and treatment.“This laboratory allows us to conduct most blood tests right at the medical camp. Now we can run laboratory tests on-site, get results quickly and begin managing patients without unnecessary delays,” he said.The Indo-Africa Charitable Society, a charitable organisation registered held at Hotel Africana in Kampala on Friday.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Byekwaso said the contribution reflects the bank’s belief that financial institutions have a broader responsibility beyond providing banking services.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We believe that banking goes beyond providing financial services to transforming lives, strengthening communities and creating opportunities for those who need them most,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Bank strengthens health investment through CSR\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Byekwaso said the bank allocates 1.5% of its previous year’s profits annually to CSR programmes focusing on health, education, environmental stewardship, community development and the social mission of the church.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Health, he noted, remains the bank’s flagship CSR pillar because healthy communities are essential for economic growth.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“A healthy population can learn, work, approved five pesticides considered by many to be PFAS \"forever chemicals,\" a class of toxic substances facing bans and increasing restrictions around the world.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>But the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has an alternative definition of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances that excludes the new herbicides, insecticides and fungicides, and says they pose no threat to human health.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">The last three such approvals were made without press statements, surfacing only when nonprofits publicized them this month.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">Many scientists and nonprofit groups say the chemicals may pose hidden risks, and many of them break down into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), now abundant in global drinking water and potentially linked to serious harms, including fetal and reproductive damage.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">\"If we want to do something about this class of chemicals, then you need to draw boundaries,\" Cindy Hu, an environmental scientist at George Washington University told AFP.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Damning history\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>PFAS are defined by the carbon-fluorine bond, the most stable in organic chemistry, whose strength and liquid repelling properties made the chemicals prized for firefighting foam, nonstick pans, raincoats and more.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">But evidence linking them to cancers, immune conditions and reproductive harms has triggered billion-dollar settlements, new laws and corporate phase-outs.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) adopted a broad definition in 2021 encompassing any molecule with a single fully-fluorinated carbon atom. Trump's second term has added five more.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">Trump's EPA says pesticides are essential for food abundance, that all are reviewed, and that single-fluorinated ones can be less toxic than alternatives. It notes they are also registered or proposed in the European Union, Canada and Australia.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">\u003Cstrong>'Getting worse'\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>That is not good enough for many scientists and activists, who fear a growing threat to the food supply and to farm workers.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">Trifludimoxazin, one of the new herbicides, has \"suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential,\" the EPA's own review found.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">And the new approvals are just the tip of the iceberg: a 2024 retrospective analysis revisited hundreds of pesticide ingredients approved in the past and found 66 would have met the OECD definition of PFAS.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">\"It's an issue that most administrations have kind of conveniently swept under the rug,\" Nathan Donley of the Center for Biological Diversity, who led the study, told AFP. \"But it's definitely getting worse.\"\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">\"If you were to buy 10 peaches or plums at random in the US, chances are nine of them are going to have at least residues of highly toxic PFAS pesticides,\" Varun Subramaniam, an Environmental Working Group scientist who conducted an analysis of produce samples, told AFP.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">Many such pesticides break down into TFA, which is now found extensively in water, and the EU's food safety agency last week sharply cut the acceptable daily intake. Since returning to power, President Donald Trump's administration has approved five pesticides considered by many to be PFAS \"forever chemicals,\" a class of toxic substances facing bans and increasing restrictions around the world.But the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has an alternative definition of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances that excludes the new herbicides, insecticides and fungicides, and says they pose no threat to human health.The last three such approvals were made without press statements, surfacing only when nonprofits publicized them this month.Many scientists and nonprofit groups say the chemicals may pose hidden risks, and many of them break down into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), now abundant in global drinking water and potentially linked to serious harms, including fetal and reproductive damage.\"If we want to do something about this class of chemicals, then you need to draw boundaries,\" Cindy Hu, an environmental scientist at George Washington University told AFP.Damning historyPFAS are defined by the carbon-fluorine bond, the most stable in organic chemistry, whose strength and liquid repelling properties made the chemicals prized for firefighting foam, nonstick pans, raincoats and more.But evidence linking them to cancers, immune conditions and reproductive harms has triggered billion-dollar settlements, new laws and corporate phase-outs.The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) adopted a broad definition in 2021 encompassing any molecule with a single fully-fluorinated carbon atom. Roughly half of US states, Congress and the Pentagon have upheld it, as did 150 scientists in a 2024 consensus statement.In 2023, the EPA under then-president Joe Biden went its own way, narrowing the definition to only include chemicals with two or more adjacent fully-fluorinated carbon atoms, which it deemed less likely to persist.One such pesticide was greenlit under Biden. Trump's second term has added five more.Trump's EPA says pesticides are essential for food abundance, that all are reviewed, and that single-fluorinated ones can be less toxic than alternatives. It notes they are also registered or proposed in the European Union, Canada and Australia.'Getting worse'That is not good enough for many scientists and activists, who fear a growing threat to the food supply and to farm workers.Trifludimoxazin, one of the new herbicides, has \"suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential,\" the EPA's own review found.And the new approvals are just the tip of the iceberg: a 2024 retrospective analysis revisited hundreds of pesticide ingredients approved in the past and found 66 would have met the OECD definition of PFAS.\"It's an issue that most administrations have kind of conveniently swept under the rug,\" Nathan Donley of the Center for Biological Diversity, who led the study, told AFP. \"But it's definitely getting worse.\"\"If you were to buy 10 peaches or plums at random in the US, chances are nine of them are going to have at least residues of highly toxic PFAS pesticides,\" Varun Subramaniam, an Environmental Working Group scientist who conducted an analysis of produce samples, told AFP.Many such pesticides break down into TFA, which is now found extensively in water, and the EU's food safety agency last week sharply cut the acceptable daily intake. In June, the European Chemicals Agency classified TFAs as toxic to reproduction, in a non-binding opinion based on animal studies.Ex-lobbyistsCriticism has focused on former lobbyists in senior EPA posts.A Freedom of Information Act request led by Donley found those officials, alongside EPA chief Lee Zeldin, coordinated edits last November to the agency's webpage on PFAS and pesticides, stripping out any acknowledgment of the more widely-accepted definition.The edit came the same day CropLife America, the pesticide industry's trade association, submitted a paper arguing against further regulation that cited the revised page. CropLife America told AFP it did not coordinate with the EPA over the timing of its submission, but rather re-submitted its manuscript to reference the revised page.For researcher Hu, the debate echoes an earlier chapter in the PFAS story. 14pt;\">\u003Cstrong>_______________\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni has paid glowing tribute to the late Dr William Sikyewunda as a courageous medical professional whose leadership was instrumental in the fight against the deadly Ebola outbreak that hit Bundibugyo district in 2007.\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>Speaking during his burial, Museveni, in an eulogy delivered on his behalf by State Minister for Lands, Harriet Ntabazi, hailed the former Bundibugyo district health officer for his lifelong commitment to saving lives and serving the people.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/2b11f637-98f4-4b44-8c96-3dbe9c93be28.jpg\" alt=\"Harriet Ntabazi delivers the President's speech. (Photo by Jonan Tusingwire)\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Harriet Ntabazi delivers the President's speech. (Photo by Jonan Tusingwire)\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He ​described Sikyewunda as a distinguished medical practitioner who dedicated his career to improving healthcare and stood at the forefront of one of the district's greatest public health emergencies.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"His legacy of service and hard work will remain an inspiration to the present and future generations,\" said the President.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As district health officer, Sikyewunda played a leading role in coordinating the response to the Ebola outbreak that was confirmed by the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO) on November 29, 2007.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The outbreak, later identified as the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, spread rapidly across the district. By early January 2008, more than 176 people had been infected, while 36 people, including five health workers, had died.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Despite the danger posed by the highly infectious disease, Sikyewunda remained on the frontline, working alongside fellow health workers, the Ministry of Health, WHO, and other partners to contain the outbreak.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Museveni ​said his calm leadership, professionalism, and commitment during the crisis helped strengthen the district's response and gave hope to communities devastated by the epidemic.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Beyond his contribution to the Ebola response, Sikyewunda also served as the Member of Parliament for Bundibugyo district between 1980 and 1985, where he was recognized for championing the welfare of his constituents.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Museveni urged young people to emulate leaders like Sikyewunda, saying they should learn from elders who dedicated their lives to serving others.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/ee3cb26a-3dff-493e-83e6-2744950883bd.jpg\" alt=\"Police officers escort the casket to the burial grounds. (Photo by Jonan Tusingwire)\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Police officers escort the casket to the burial grounds. But Dr Sikyewunda came up with an initiative in the council and proposed that all doctors posted to the district be given an extra sh1 million in addition to their salaries. \u003Cstrong>MEVAC, a private veterinary vaccine manufacturing facility in Egypt, is set to establish a Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) vaccine manufacturing factory in Nakyesasa, Wakiso district.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Agriculture minister Frank Tumwebaze revealed on Tuesday (July 28) that the company had completed all preliminary procedures and made a final investment decision for the establishment of the Uganda FMD vaccine factory.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He made the announcement on his official X account after leading his team on a visit and tour of what he described as the company’s high-tech infrastructure.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The minister described MEVAC as a leading animal vaccine manufacturing company in the Middle East and a subsidiary of the Egyptian Ministry of Defence.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“This is the same entity designated by the government of Egypt to come and establish an FMD manufacturing facility in Uganda under the G2G partnership. I congratulate MeVAC company for their advanced R and D innovations and thank them for having concluded all the preliminary procedures and made a final investment decision for the Uganda FMD vaccine factory,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“The FMD vaccine will be constructed at the Nakyesasa @narouganda (National Agricultural Research Organisation) campus next to the anti-tick vaccine [facility]. Gradually, a vaccine city will be born at Namulonge along Gayaza Road.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Tumwebaze and his team are in Cairo, Egypt, to advance several agreed agricultural projects between the two countries.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The projects cover areas including fish and poultry farming, agricultural research, and the establishment of an FMD vaccine manufacturing factory in Wakiso.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The delegation arrived in Cairo on July 26, 2026, to meet Egyptian officials and discuss clear strategies and timelines for implementing the projects.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Upon arrival, the minister said on his X account that the visit was part of efforts to follow up on decisions made by the two heads of state in Kampala in May this year during Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s state visit.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/3f4c4da0-816b-4afa-89b2-3f667b12e355.jpg\" alt=\"The minister noted that Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, for efforts made through his military diplomatic relations with Egypt.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The minister noted that Gen. Gradually, a vaccine city will be born at Namulonge along Gayaza Road.”Tumwebaze and his team are in Cairo, Egypt, to advance several agreed agricultural projects between the two countries.The projects cover areas including fish and poultry farming, agricultural research, and the establishment of an FMD vaccine manufacturing factory in Wakiso.The delegation arrived in Cairo on July 26, 2026, to meet Egyptian officials and discuss clear strategies and timelines for implementing the projects.Upon arrival, the minister said on his X account that the visit was part of efforts to follow up on decisions made by the two heads of state in Kampala in May this year during Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s state visit.“One of the advanced collaboration projects we hope to sign and conclude during this visit is the setting up of timelines for the groundbreaking of the FMD [vaccine] manufacturing factory in Uganda,” he said.Tumwebaze thanked Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces, Gen. 14pt;\">Uganda is officially Ebola free, the health minister, Dr Chris Baryomunsi, has announced.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"This confirmation comes after the country discharged the Two patients died, giving the country a case fatality rate of about 10%, significantly lower than the more than 30% typically associated with the Ebola Bundibugyo virus outbreaks.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The World Health Organisation has attributed Uganda's success to years of investment in epidemic preparedness, including specialised treatment facilities, trained emergency medical teams and pre-positioned medical supplies.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>However, officials warn that Uganda's risk remains high because transmission continues across the border. Baryomunsi said surveillance has been intensified along communities stretching from West Nile to Kisoro while health workers continue screening travellers and educating border communities about Ebola prevention.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Congolese health authorities, the country has now recorded over 2,300\u003Cstrong> \u003C/strong>confirmed Ebola cases, including 930 deaths, with the outbreak continuing to outpace response efforts in some affected areas\u003C/p>","_________________Uganda is officially Ebola free, the health minister, Dr Chris Baryomunsi, has announced.\"This confirmation comes after the country discharged the last Ugandan national on June 16, 2026,\" Baryomunsi said in a statement on his X handle on Tuesday, July 28, 2026.Unlike previous Ebola outbreaks that informed the current 42-day declaration policy, the minister said Uganda’s 2026 Ebola outbreak arose from a fully documented importation event.\"The source of infection was identified, the route of introduction established, all confirmed cases were epidemiologically linked, transmission chains were completely characterised and reconstructed, and all identified contacts were institutionally quarantined and completed the mandatory 21-day follow-up without evidence of further transmission,\" he stated.Baryomunsi revealed that enhanced surveillance has detected no unexplained community transmission.Uganda's latest outbreak infected 20 people, including 15 Congolese nationals, four health workers and one driver. Two patients died, giving the country a case fatality rate of about 10%, significantly lower than the more than 30% typically associated with the Ebola Bundibugyo virus outbreaks.The World Health Organisation has attributed Uganda's success to years of investment in epidemic preparedness, including specialised treatment facilities, trained emergency medical teams and pre-positioned medical supplies.However, officials warn that Uganda's risk remains high because transmission continues across the border. 14pt;\">DETROIT - \u003Cstrong>US Democrats vote Tuesday in their marquee primary in Michigan, choosing between a left-wing insurgent and an establishment-backed congresswoman in a contest that has become a proxy war over Israel, electability and the future of the national party.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The winner will face former Republican congressman Mike Rogers in November for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, a race central to the party's difficult effort to win control of the Senate.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Democrats must defend Michigan while gaining four Republican-held seats to control the upper chamber, making the primary more than an ideological exercise in a state that has swung between the two parties in recent national elections.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Analysts say the results will show whether a current leftist surge among Democrats can move beyond party safe seats and win in battlegrounds with national consequences -- or whether Michigan's Democratic establishment can still hold the line.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Abdul El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director backed by leftist leaders Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has cast himself as a working-class fighter willing to confront corporations, party leaders and increasingly unpopular pro-Israel donors.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Haley Stevens, a four-term lawmaker from the Detroit suburbs, has built her campaign around experience, manufacturing and electability. She is supported by establishment figures from Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer to Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Israel divide\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Several recent polls have shown El-Sayed ahead, raising the prospect of the left's biggest victory yet in a primary season marked by a series of anti-establishment wins.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>His allies say the campaign's volunteer energy proves progressives can build a statewide coalition without relying on Washington's traditional donor network.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Momentum doesn't happen by accident,\" said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the grassroots group Our Revolution, which says its volunteers have made more than 300,000 voter contacts for El-Sayed.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Stevens is counting on support that she says may be underrepresented in opinion polls -- from Black voters, older Democrats and people without college degrees.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bitterest divide has been over the United States' deep support for Israel.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Stevens has defended continued military backing for the country and rejected accusations that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>El-Sayed has called for an end to unconditional US aid, attacked the influence of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) lobby group, and said Israel should not exist specifically as a Jewish state.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>AIPAC spending and outside advertising totaling $90 million -- in a state with a large Arab American population and deep anger over the Gaza war -- has made Michigan another national test of the pro-Israel lobby's ability to shape Democratic primaries.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>'Brutality'\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>The candidates have traded increasingly personal attacks, with El-Sayed calling Stevens \"the least capable candidate in America,\" while she has accused him of blaming his problems on Jewish Americans.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, who has remained neutral, warned that the \"brutality\" and \"ugliness\" of the campaign could make it harder for Democrats to unite afterward.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Both camps insist their candidate offers the stronger path against However, several key concerns in your article require scrutiny if Uganda is to design a policy that balances industrial growth with genuine environmental protection.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">The Voluntary Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) systems are not a substitute for regulation. Uganda’s voluntary schemes suffer from parasitism. Manufacturers not party to such systems bear no responsibility, and there are no legally binding collection or recycling targets. Your article boasts a future ambition of 75% recycling in eight years, yet no independent audit verifies current rates. Proper management requires mandatory Extended Producer Responsibility with enforceable penalties, public reporting, and integration of informal waste collectors, none of which you clearly addressed.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">Problematic non‑recyclable plastics are also ignored. Not all plastics are equal. Their differences in as far as this response is concerned are in chemical structure and recyclability. Multilayer laminates and thin carrier bags are unrecyclable in Uganda’s current infrastructure. The claims have always been that they clog sorting machines and consequently find their way into drainage channels or open burning. The Kiteezi landfill incident cannot be overemphasized. By your article defending all plastics uniformly, it sidesteps the need to phase out or tax specifically those plastics that have no circular pathway in Uganda’s current infrastructure.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">The regional comparisons cited are selective. You noted that Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda offer lower excise duties on raw materials, but you leave out the fact that Kenya enforces one of Africa’s strictest plastic bag bans and mandatory Sustainable Waste Management (Extended Producer Responsibility) Regulations, 2024 under Legal Notice No. 176. Rwanda has prohibited single‑use plastics entirely since 2008 and currently enforcing the ban under Law No. 17/2019. These countries pair fiscal incentives with strong command and control instruments to enforce compliance through fines, penalties, and mandatory standards rather than incentives.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">The inflationary burden argument in Paragraph Sixteen ignores environmental costs. While you for example cite a potential 25% price increase for a water sachet, from sh200 to sh250, it is regrettable that you do not calculate the cost of unmanaged waste. Among others, this includes flooded drainage, wetland destruction, veterinary and human health effects from microplastics. Those costs are also borne by the low‑income Ugandans you referred to, often invisibly. Proper management internalizes unintended consequences through well designed levies, but not by ignoring them.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">Your data lacks independent verification. Claims of 105,000 tonnes recycled annually, $120 million invested, and 350,000 livelihoods depend on self-reporting done by Uganda Manufacturers Association members. As revealed by Dr. Akankwasa Barirega, Director at the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA), ahead of World Environment Day 2025, Uganda generates around 600 metric tons of plastic waste each day, an estimate of about 219,000 tonnes a year. NEMA noted as of May, 2022 that only 5% is recycled annually in Uganda. With the noted percentage from NEMA in 2022, it seems miraculous that as of 2026, 48% of NEMA’s reported annual 219,000 tonnes a year in plastic waste is being recycled. Significant gaps remain between claimed recycling and actual environmental leakage.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">The plastics industry is an economic asset, but unmanaged waste is a mounting liability. We urge Uganda Manufacturers Association to work with government on an evidence‑based fiscal framework rather than defending an untenable status quo. We must embrace a balanced and enforceable regulation.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 12pt;\">\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>The writer is Project Manager/Staff Advocate, Greenwatch\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003C/p>","_____________OPINIONBy Mpewo Alan CollinsGreenwatch appreciates your concern regarding the proposed excise duty on plastic raw materials in your article published in the New Vision newspaper dated Thursday, May 28, 2026, on page 11. Your article rightly noted in Paragraph One that poor waste management, and not plastics per se, is the root cause of environmental pollution. However, several key concerns in your article require scrutiny if Uganda is to design a policy that balances industrial growth with genuine environmental protection.The Voluntary Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) systems are not a substitute for regulation. Uganda’s voluntary schemes suffer from parasitism. Manufacturers not party to such systems bear no responsibility, and there are no legally binding collection or recycling targets. Your article boasts a future ambition of 75% recycling in eight years, yet no independent audit verifies current rates. Proper management requires mandatory Extended Producer Responsibility with enforceable penalties, public reporting, and integration of informal waste collectors, none of which you clearly addressed.Problematic non‑recyclable plastics are also ignored. Not all plastics are equal. Their differences in as far as this response is concerned are in chemical structure and recyclability. Multilayer laminates and thin carrier bags are unrecyclable in Uganda’s current infrastructure. The claims have always been that they clog sorting machines and consequently find their way into drainage channels or open burning. The Kiteezi landfill incident cannot be overemphasized. By your article defending all plastics uniformly, it sidesteps the need to phase out or tax specifically those plastics that have no circular pathway in Uganda’s current infrastructure.The regional comparisons cited are selective. You noted that Kenya, Tanzania, and Rwanda offer lower excise duties on raw materials, but you leave out the fact that Kenya enforces one of Africa’s strictest plastic bag bans and mandatory Sustainable Waste Management (Extended Producer Responsibility) Regulations, 2024 under Legal Notice No. 176. Rwanda has prohibited single‑use plastics entirely since 2008 and currently enforcing the ban under Law No. 17/2019. These countries pair fiscal incentives with strong command and control instruments to enforce compliance through fines, penalties, and mandatory standards rather than incentives.The inflationary burden argument in Paragraph Sixteen ignores environmental costs. While you for example cite a potential 25% price increase for a water sachet, from sh200 to sh250, it is regrettable that you do not calculate the cost of unmanaged waste. Among others, this includes flooded drainage, wetland destruction, veterinary and human health effects from microplastics. Those costs are also borne by the low‑income Ugandans you referred to, often invisibly. Proper management internalizes unintended consequences through well designed levies, but not by ignoring them.Your data lacks independent verification. Claims of 105,000 tonnes recycled annually, $120 million invested, and 350,000 livelihoods depend on self-reporting done by Uganda Manufacturers Association members. As revealed by Dr. Akankwasa Barirega, Director at the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA), ahead of World Environment Day 2025, Uganda generates around 600 metric tons of plastic waste each day, an estimate of about 219,000 tonnes a year. NEMA noted as of May, 2022 that only 5% is recycled annually in Uganda. With the noted percentage from NEMA in 2022, it seems miraculous that as of 2026, 48% of NEMA’s reported annual 219,000 tonnes a year in plastic waste is being recycled. Significant gaps remain between claimed recycling and actual environmental leakage.The plastics industry is an economic asset, but unmanaged waste is a mounting liability. We urge Uganda Manufacturers Association to work with government on an evidence‑based fiscal framework rather than defending an untenable status quo. Uganda can industrialize and clean its environment simultaneously, but only if all parties abandon selective data. We must embrace a balanced and enforceable regulation.The writer is Project Manager/Staff Advocate, Greenwatch","The plastics industry is an economic asset, but unmanaged waste is a mounting liability. 19:23:33","Why Africa is rallying for new tax rules","why-africa-is-rallying-for-new-tax-rules","\u003Cp>_______________\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">As the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) on the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation (UNFCITC) kicks off the latest negotiations from 3rd to 13th August in New York, Africa is rallying for better tax rules, especially as bilateral and multilateral agreements take precedence over domestic tax laws.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>With the negotiations bending into the last miles, since 2022, African countries anticipate favourable outcomes, including a clear UN Convention and fair rules on tax dispute resolution, as the continent loses an estimated $483 billion, according to Tax Justice Network Africa (TJNA), to, among others, porous double taxation agreements amidst limited arbitration capacity where transfer pricing arises.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Heading into the negotiations, the Global Alliance for Tax Justice has already set the tempo. According to Chenai Mukumba, the Executive Director at TJNA, the process is fundamentally about reclaiming Africa’s economic sovereignty.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Africa’s labour, natural resources, and markets have generated enormous wealth yet the international tax rules have often denied African countries their fair share of taxing rights over the arising income,” she says.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>UNFCITC promises fair allocation of taxing rights. However, although the early protocols to the Convention are focused on the taxation of income from cross-border services and the prevention and resolution of tax disputes, Tove Maria Ryding, the tax coordinator at the European Network on Debt and Development (EURODAD), notes that neither of the protocols have a clear objective at the moment.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Scenario, Demands\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Africa is keen to divorce the OECD in favour of the UN, which promises a dedicated body to address tax-related matters, anticipating fair international tax rules even where countries have limited treaty networks, while also fixing limits to improved domestic resource mobilisation.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Developed countries keep claiming a duplication of rules, citing the existence of the OECD framework. But Africa reiterates that such rules are outdated and unfit for purpose. If African governments can’t effectively tax the multi-billion-dollar multinational enterprises, they will resort to increasing Pay As You Earn and other taxes,” says Dr Zandile Ndebele, a policy officer at TJNA.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to the African Group, the protocol on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes should establish minimum standards and optional mechanisms for the prevention and resolution of cross‑border tax disputes that arise from bilateral or multilateral tax agreements between parties.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“African countries face complex cross-border tax challenges in an increasingly globalised economy. Existing mechanisms and frameworks for cross-border tax dispute prevention and resolution have often favoured jurisdictions with greater technical capacity and broader treaty networks, leaving many African States exposed to prolonged tax disputes, revenue loss, and legal uncertainties,” the African Group observes.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Background\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>In December 2022, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution to promote inclusive and effective international tax cooperation to further commitments that also seek to fix illicit financial flows, where Africa loses an estimated $88.6b per year, combat aggressive tax avoidance and evasion.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The move follows persistent demands to amend the existing treaty-based rules, which unfairly allocate rights to tax income and capital among jurisdictions, over time enabling aspects like profit shifting, thus motivating the need for change to reflect new ways that business may be conducted in an increasingly digitalised and globalised economy.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>The Tax Disputes\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>African countries no longer want physical presence of multinational enterprises to be the basis of taxation, a factor which shapes the dispute scenario. Still, they intend to ensure that non‑treaty disputes remain outside the scope of the UN Framework instrument, giving power to domestic arbitration whenever it’s required.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As for the current tax system, the continent still sits on the receiving end while tied to porous double taxation agreements. Mark Mutumba, a trade policy analyst, explains that as taxing rights, based on source of revenue and residence of corporations shape arising disputes, the protocol on prevention and resolution of tax disputes now offers a wide range of options. For instance, joint and simultaneous audits, the mutual agreement procedure, conciliation and mediation, besides arbitration.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Even in the absence of double taxation agreements with countries like Australia and France, if Uganda ratifies the second protocol, it can tap into the wider web of dispute resolution. However, the political will shall define the success of the negotiations,” says Mutumba\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Uganda’s Landing Point\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>Aloysious Kittengo, the programme coordinator, financing for development, at the Southern and Eastern Africa Trade Information and Negotiations Institute cites an opportunity for Uganda. “The existing tax system favours capital flight and the ultra-wealthy. Uganda now has an opportunity to change this by demanding a fair share of the tax revenue from the operations of multinational corporations,” says Kittengo.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Uganda’s transfer pricing regulations, 2011, are drawn from the OECD framework. However, Mutumba highlights gaps like the long time frame and non-binding nature of the mutual agreement procedure, plus a lack of arbitration to the end, which is also costly for many African countries.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Whereas Uganda's 9 double taxation agreements with countries like the United Kingdom, Netherlands, India, and South Africa generally limit its ability to tax dividends, interest, royalties, technical fees and other derivatives, the same treaties are invoked in times of investor-state dispute due to the excessive leverage they extend to the developed country investors.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For instance, in the arbitration between Tullow Uganda and the Republic of Uganda, the Uganda-UK double taxation agreement served as the legal instrument. As for Total E&P BV Vs Republic of Uganda, the Netherlands-Uganda treaty was used. Kittengo explains that the majority of the foreign investors in Uganda come from complicated jurisdictions that undermine transfer pricing and the arm’s length principle.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Meanwhile, the fact that countries can opt in or out of the protocol on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes has been raised as a risky turning point that’s likely to undermine the Convention's intentions. Still, the protocol discussions have been quoted to be disconnected from the Convention.\u003C/p>","_______________As the Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC) on the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation (UNFCITC) kicks off the latest negotiations from 3rd to 13th August in New York, Africa is rallying for better tax rules, especially as bilateral and multilateral agreements take precedence over domestic tax laws.With the negotiations bending into the last miles, since 2022, African countries anticipate favourable outcomes, including a clear UN Convention and fair rules on tax dispute resolution, as the continent loses an estimated $483 billion, according to Tax Justice Network Africa (TJNA), to, among others, porous double taxation agreements amidst limited arbitration capacity where transfer pricing arises.Heading into the negotiations, the Global Alliance for Tax Justice has already set the tempo. According to Chenai Mukumba, the Executive Director at TJNA, the process is fundamentally about reclaiming Africa’s economic sovereignty.“Africa’s labour, natural resources, and markets have generated enormous wealth yet the international tax rules have often denied African countries their fair share of taxing rights over the arising income,” she says.UNFCITC promises fair allocation of taxing rights. However, although the early protocols to the Convention are focused on the taxation of income from cross-border services and the prevention and resolution of tax disputes, Tove Maria Ryding, the tax coordinator at the European Network on Debt and Development (EURODAD), notes that neither of the protocols have a clear objective at the moment.Scenario, DemandsAfrica is keen to divorce the OECD in favour of the UN, which promises a dedicated body to address tax-related matters, anticipating fair international tax rules even where countries have limited treaty networks, while also fixing limits to improved domestic resource mobilisation.“Developed countries keep claiming a duplication of rules, citing the existence of the OECD framework. But Africa reiterates that such rules are outdated and unfit for purpose. If African governments can’t effectively tax the multi-billion-dollar multinational enterprises, they will resort to increasing Pay As You Earn and other taxes,” says Dr Zandile Ndebele, a policy officer at TJNA.According to the African Group, the protocol on the prevention and resolution of tax disputes should establish minimum standards and optional mechanisms for the prevention and resolution of cross‑border tax disputes that arise from bilateral or multilateral tax agreements between parties.“African countries face complex cross-border tax challenges in an increasingly globalised economy. Limited grew its balance sheet in the first half of 2026, with customer deposits and lending posting double-digit growth even as the bank slipped to a Shs15.8 billion loss after tax.\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>The bank’s total assets rose to Shs3.94 trillion by June 30, 2026, up from the corresponding period last year, driven by stronger customer deposits and an expanding loan book.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Customer deposits increased to Shs2.87 trillion from Shs2.46 trillion a year earlier, while advances to customers grew to Shs1.44 trillion from Shs1.19 trillion, representing growth of about 21%.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The figures point to continued business activity, with dfcu attracting more customer funds and extending additional credit during the period.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The unaudited half-year results show that customer deposits rose by about Shs410 billion, giving the bank a stronger funding base.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>At the same time, borrowings declined to Shs200.4 billion from about Shs255 billion a year earlier, reflecting a greater reliance on customer deposits to support operations and lending.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bank’s liquidity position also remained solid.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Liquid assets stood at Shs2.18 trillion at the end of June, while cash and cash equivalents amounted to Shs662.7 billion.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>dfcu also maintained a strong capital position, with both core and total capital ratios reported at 27%. Shareholders’ equity stood at Shs755.4 billion.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bank’s advances to customers grew by about 21% to Shs1.44 trillion, signalling continued demand for credit from households and businesses.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>However, the expansion in lending came with an impairment allowance of Shs11.8 billion on loans and advances, emphasizing the need for continued vigilance on asset quality as the bank grows its loan book.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bank reported net income of Shs215.6 billion in the six months, up from Shs199.4 billion in the same period last year.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>But operating expenses rose sharply to Shs230 billion from Shs150.4 billion, putting pressure on profitability.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Together with the Shs11.8 billion impairment allowance, the higher cost base pushed the bank into a pre-tax loss of Shs26.3 billion, compared with a profit before tax of Shs39.7 billion in the first half of 2025.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>An income tax credit of Shs10.5 billion reduced the loss after tax to Shs15.8 billion.\u003Cbr>Despite the earnings pressure, dfcu’s capital and liquidity position provide important support as the bank works to restore profitability.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>With Shs2.18 trillion in liquid assets, Shs755.4 billion in shareholders’ equity and capital ratios of 27%, the lender remains well placed to continue operations and support credit growth.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The results also show continued expansion in the bank’s core funding base, with deposits rising even as borrowings declined.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The half-year performance presents a mixed picture of strong balance-sheet growth on one hand, and pressure on earnings on the other.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The increase in deposits, lending and assets points to continued expansion, while the rise in operating expenses highlights the need for tighter cost control.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bank will also need to protect the quality of its growing loan book as it seeks to deepen lending and improve results in the second half of the year.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For customers and businesses, the growth in deposits and advances suggests that dfcu remains active in mobilising savings and extending credit to the economy.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Separately, dfcu Bank welcomed a ruling delivered on 23 July 2026 by the English Commercial Court in the ongoing proceedings brought by Crane Bank Limited and others against dfcu Bank and other parties. \u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The decision marks a significant procedural victory for the bank after claimants sought to challenge the forensic reports and prevent dfcu Bank from relying on those documents at trial. \u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In a previous judgment, the Court decided that those reports will be in evidence at trial. The Court’s latest decision means that the two PwC witnesses who led the teams who prepared these reports will be heard at trial.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>PwC was engaged by the Bank of Uganda after Crane Bank entered statutory management to prepare an inventory of Crane Bank’s assets and liabilities and, separately, to conduct a forensic review into Crane Bank. \u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The inventory indicated that Crane Bank was significantly undercapitalised, while the forensic review identified several issues relating to Crane Bank’s historic management.\u003C/p>","KAMPALA - dfcu Limited grew its balance sheet in the first half of 2026, with customer deposits and lending posting double-digit growth even as the bank slipped to a Shs15.8 billion loss after tax.The bank’s total assets rose to Shs3.94 trillion by June 30, 2026, up from the corresponding period last year, driven by stronger customer deposits and an expanding loan book.Customer deposits increased to Shs2.87 trillion from Shs2.46 trillion a year earlier, while advances to customers grew to Shs1.44 trillion from Shs1.19 trillion, representing growth of about 21%.The figures point to continued business activity, with dfcu attracting more customer funds and extending additional credit during the period.The unaudited half-year results show that customer deposits rose by about Shs410 billion, giving the bank a stronger funding base.At the same time, borrowings declined to Shs200.4 billion from about Shs255 billion a year earlier, reflecting a greater reliance on customer deposits to support operations and lending.The bank’s liquidity position also remained solid.Liquid assets stood at Shs2.18 trillion at the end of June, while cash and cash equivalents amounted to Shs662.7 billion.dfcu also maintained a strong capital position, with both core and total capital ratios reported at 27%. bank reported net income of Shs215.6 billion in the six months, up from Shs199.4 billion in the same period last year.But operating expenses rose sharply to Shs230 billion from Shs150.4 billion, provide important support as the bank works to restore profitability.With Shs2.18 trillion in liquid assets, Shs755.4 billion in shareholders’ equity and capital ratios of 27%, the lender remains well placed to continue operations and support credit growth.The results also show continued expansion in the bank’s core funding base, with deposits rising even as borrowings declined.The half-year performance presents a mixed picture of strong balance-sheet growth on one hand, and pressure on earnings on the other.The increase in deposits, lending and assets points to continued expansion, while the rise in operating expenses highlights the need for tighter cost control.The bank will also need to protect the quality of its growing loan book as it seeks to deepen lending and improve results in the second half of the year.For customers and businesses, the growth in deposits and advances suggests that dfcu remains active in mobilising savings and extending credit to the economy.Separately, dfcu Bank welcomed a ruling delivered on 23 July 2026 by the English Commercial Court in the ongoing proceedings brought by Crane Bank Limited and others against dfcu Bank and other parties. We support farmers through improved seed, soil and water conservation, agroforestry, integrated soil fertility management, water harvesting and other climate-resilient practices.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>We have supported Climate-Smart Villages in Nakaseke and other areas as practical learning hubs where farmers can test and adopt technologies.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>One of the key lessons is that climate-smart agriculture is most effective when combined with strong farmer organisations, access to markets and sustainable service delivery systems.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Through our Commercial Community-Based Facilitator model, farmers receive continuous coaching and technical support close to their communities.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>Q: What about post-harvest losses and aflatoxin contamination?\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>A: Poor post-harvest handling remains a significant challenge, reducing food quality, threatening public health and limiting farmers’ access to premium markets.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>We train farmers in proper harvesting, drying, sorting, grading, storage and safe handling. We must strengthen every ecosystem actor - from research institutions and extension providers to seed companies, financial institutions, processors, traders, cooperatives, government agencies and development partners.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The future of Uganda’s agriculture lies not only in producing more, but in building resilient, inclusive and competitive agri-food systems that create value for farmers, businesses and communities.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>By scaling innovation and strengthening ecosystem partnerships, we can create lasting impact that benefits farmers, businesses, communities and future generations.\u003C/p>","_______________Robert Anyang, Country Director of Sasakawa Africa Association Uganda, speaks to New Vision about the barriers holding back smallholder farmers and the systems needed to turn them into profitable agripreneurs.
