12:31:00","BoU takes financial literacy campaign to schools, churches","bou-takes-financial-literacy-campaign-to-scho","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">KAMPALA - \u003Cstrong>The Bank of Uganda (BoU) will expand its financial literacy campaign to schools, churches, financial institutions and communities across the country as it seeks to build a stronger saving culture and improve Ugandans' understanding of money management.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba said the initiative forms part of activities marking the central bank's 60th anniversary, aimed at equipping Ugandans of all ages with knowledge about saving, responsible financial management and the country's financial system.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We are going to engage schools, churches and other religious institutions. We shall also bring on board commercial banks, insurance companies, fintechs and mobile money institutions so that everyone participates in building a stronger economy.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/dfb4277b-1a30-41aa-97bd-5ef87c9b8f17.jpg\" alt=\"Gibril Rwenzaho of Wakiso Junior School who emerged the overall winner with the dummy check, on the right is Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba and left is his trainer Peter Bwengye.\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Gibril Rwenzaho of Wakiso Junior School who emerged the overall winner with the dummy check, on the right is Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba and left is his trainer Peter Bwengye.\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He said the campaign was driven by concerns that many Ugandans still have weak saving habits, making financial literacy a priority for the central bank.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“The problem we have in Uganda largely is a poor saving culture. By engaging children at that early stage, we are building values of saving, respecting money and investing wisely,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“As they grow, they become responsible citizens who can make sound financial decisions.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Prof. Nuwagaba was speaking during the judging ceremony of the Bank of Uganda @60 Primary Schools Poetry Competition held at the Bank’s headquarters in Kampala on July 29, 2026.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/7348f7df-3380-43ad-9d15-90dc147e5ae9.jpg\" alt=\"First runner-up Lenity Manzi of Banyatereza Golden Jubilee Memorial School.\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>First runner-up Lenity Manzi of Banyatereza Golden Jubilee Memorial School.\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The championship challenged primary school pupils to write poems on the benefits of saving money, proper handling of Uganda’s currency and the importance of using regulated financial institutions.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>It attracted 3,390 entries from pupils across more than 40 districts, and judges shortlisted 192 poems before selecting 22 finalists who performed during the event.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Responsible money habits\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>Bank of Uganda Director Currency Christine B. Alupo said teaching children about money at an early age was important because financial habits are often formed during childhood.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Children absorb habits far more easily than adults, and money habits are no exception. At primary level, a child is already handling coins and notes, whether it is break time cash or contributions to a class project, so this is not a distant future skill. It is something they need now,” she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/5bb7a44d-0c69-48cc-924b-f05ef1c0f708.jpeg\" alt=\"Christine Alupo (L), Director Currency, and Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba (C) and judges during the competitions.\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Christine Alupo (L), Director Currency, and Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba (C) and judges during the competitions.\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Alupo said helping children understand saving, responsible spending and proper currency handling would contribute to raising financially responsible citizens.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“When children understand the value of money, how to save, how to spend responsibly and how to care for currency, they grow into more financially responsible citizens,” she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She added that proper currency handling also helps protect Uganda’s banknotes by reducing damage and the cost of replacing worn-out notes.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Alupo urged children and the public to treat currency as a shared national asset, warning against practices that shorten the lifespan of banknotes.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/8ffc8e65-c37c-446c-826e-06138eda0c6e.jpeg\" alt=\"Elnathan Tumwebaze from Peak Primary school together with his teacher recieve a dummy check after emerging second runners up.\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Elnathan Tumwebaze from Peak Primary school together with his teacher recieve a dummy check after emerging second runners up.\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Some of the common mistakes we see are notes folded excessively, stapled, written on, or exposed to water, dirt and excessive heat. These habits damage the currency and shorten its lifespan,” she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She encouraged Ugandans to also familiarise themselves with security features on banknotes to help identify genuine currency.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“The message we want children to take home is simple: Know Your Money,” she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Financial lessons\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Prof. Nuwagaba said poetry was chosen as a way of making financial literacy lessons more engaging for young learners.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We believe financial literacy should begin early because the habits children develop today become the habits they carry into adulthood.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Poetry helps young learners understand important issues in an engaging and creative way,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/f4157700-583c-496b-9ed6-152de080ff03.jpeg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Peter Bwengye, a public speaking trainer at Wakiso Junior School, said the competition had helped learners build confidence while improving their communication skills.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“When children perform poems before an audience, they learn confidence, expression and public speaking. They also improve their language and become better communicators,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Schools and parents welcome initiative\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Teachers said the competition had helped make financial literacy more relatable for learners by allowing them to participate actively.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Alice Nansereko, Headteacher of Luzira Hill Parents School, said the initiative had increased children’s interest in understanding money management.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/a801f2f7-f55e-4455-a721-eba8899aea38.jpeg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Bank of Uganda has taught children how to handle money properly through poetry. They are now more interested in learning because they are actively involved,” she said.\u003Cbr>Parents also welcomed the programme, saying early lessons on saving could help children develop better financial habits.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Polly Grace Akullu, a parent from West Nile, said many families do not always teach children about saving.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“When children begin saving while they are still young, they grow up understanding the value of planning for the future,” she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The Bank of Uganda will publish the 192 shortlisted poems in an anthology as part of its 60th anniversary celebrations, preserving the children’s creative work and providing schools with a resource that can continue promoting financial literacy.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The competition crowned Gibril Rwenzaho of Wakiso Junior School as the overall winner. He received a Shs5 million bursary, while his school was awarded Shs12 million.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>First runner-up Lenity Manzi of Banyatereza Golden Jubilee Memorial School from Fort Portal received a Shs4 million bursary, while second runner-up Elnathan Tumwebaze of Peak Primary School received a Shs3 million bursary.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The winning poems will also feature in the anniversary anthology.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The poetry competition is among activities marking 60 years of the Bank of Uganda, which was established on August 15, 1966, and continues to play a role in maintaining price stability, supervising the financial sector and safeguarding the value of the Uganda Shilling.","KAMPALA - The Bank of Uganda (BoU) will expand its financial literacy campaign to schools, churches, financial institutions and communities across the country as it seeks to build a stronger saving culture and improve Ugandans' understanding of money management.Deputy Governor Prof. Augustus Nuwagaba said the initiative forms part of activities marking the central bank's 60th anniversary, aimed at equipping Ugandans of all ages with knowledge about saving, responsible financial management and the country's financial system.“We are going to engage schools, churches and other religious institutions. Court in Kampala has overturned a Sh15.3m award against Pearl Bank, formerly known as PostBank Uganda Limited, ruling that the bank was not liable for money deposited on the account of a person with a similar name to the intended beneficiary.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Justice Simon Peter Kinobe of the High Court Civil Division set aside the judgment and orders of the Mengo Chief Magistrate’s Court, which had ordered Pearl Bank to refund sh15,362,412 to William Barigye.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The magistrate had also awarded Barigye sh10m in general damages, sh5m in exemplary damages and costs of the suit.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Barigye had sued Pearl Bank, claiming that money from the Directorate of Citizenship and Immigration Control, including his salary and facilitation, had been mistakenly deposited on the account of another person, William Baligye.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He claimed that between December 2012 and June 2014, money amounting to sh15,362,412 meant for him was continuously remitted to the account of Baligye, which was held with the then PostBank, and withdrawn.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Barigye, an employee of the Directorate of Citizenship and Immigration Control in the Ministry of Internal Affairs, said he had never operated an account with PostBank and used a Centenary Bank account to receive his salary and other emoluments.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He argued that although there was a difference between the names Barigye and Baligye, the bank should have detected the error and refunded his money after the anomaly was brought to its attention.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The matter came before the High Court after Pearl Bank, formerly PostBank, appealed against the decision of the chief magistrate, arguing that the trial court had wrongly found it negligent and liable to pay exemplary damages.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In his judgment delivered on July 27, 2026, Justice Kinobe held that Barigye did not have an account with PostBank and, therefore, had no relationship with the bank.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The judge said the bank’s relationship was with the account holder, Baligye, who also used the name Barigye interchangeably.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Justice Kinobe noted that the account holder had a Uganda Police Force warrant card in the name “Barigye William” and also wrote the same name on withdrawal slips.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The court heard that PostBank received electronic funds transfers from the Bank of Uganda for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, including payments directed to account number 001030017010586, held in the name of Barigye William.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bank’s back-office manager, Norah Nagayi, testified that the bank credited the account in accordance with the instructions it received.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She also told court that the bank did not receive any complaint from Barigye or his employer between December 2008 and June 2014 concerning the alleged anomaly.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The complaint was only brought to the bank’s attention in August 2014, by which time the money had already been withdrawn.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Justice Kinobe ruled that the bank could not reasonably have foreseen that the transactions were irregular, particularly because the account holder used the name “Barigye William” on the withdrawal slips.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“It is clear from the foregoing that Barigye, the plaintiff, did not hold any account with Post Bank and so he had no relationship with the bank,” the judge ruled.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The judge added that there was no relationship of proximity between Barigye and the bank, noting that PostBank owed a duty to release the money to its account holder upon request.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He said the fact that the anomaly was raised in August 2014, long after the money had been withdrawn, meant that the bank could not be held liable for negligence.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Justice Kinobe said had the trial magistrate properly considered the evidence and the letter from the Director of Citizenship and Immigration Control, she would not have found PostBank liable.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He consequently allowed the appeal and set aside the chief magistrate’s judgment and all the orders issued on April 28, 2017.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He ordered that each party bears its own costs of the appeal.\u003C/p>","KAMPALA - The High Court in Kampala has overturned a Sh15.3m award against Pearl Bank, formerly known as PostBank Uganda Limited, ruling that the bank was not liable for money deposited on the account of a person with a similar name to the intended beneficiary.Justice Simon Peter Kinobe of the High Court Civil Division set aside the judgment and orders of the Mengo Chief Magistrate’s Court, which had ordered Pearl Bank to refund sh15,362,412 to William Barigye.The magistrate had also awarded Barigye sh10m in general damages, sh5m in exemplary damages and costs of the suit.Barigye had sued Pearl Bank, claiming that money from the Directorate of Citizenship and Immigration Control, including his salary and facilitation, had been mistakenly deposited on the account of another person, William Baligye.He claimed that between December 2012 and June 2014, money amounting to sh15,362,412 meant for him was continuously remitted to the account of Baligye, which was held with the then PostBank, and withdrawn.Barigye, an employee of the Directorate of Citizenship and Immigration Control in the Ministry of Internal Affairs, said he had never operated an account with PostBank and used a Centenary Bank account to receive his salary and other emoluments.He argued that although there was a difference between the names Barigye and Baligye, the bank should have detected the error and refunded his money after the anomaly was brought to its attention.The matter came before the High Court after Pearl Bank, formerly PostBank, appealed against the decision of the chief magistrate, arguing that the trial court had wrongly found it negligent and liable to pay exemplary damages.In his judgment delivered on July 27, 2026, Justice Kinobe held that Barigye did not have an account with PostBank and, therefore, had no relationship with the bank.The judge said the bank’s relationship was with the account holder, Baligye, who also used the name Barigye interchangeably.Justice Kinobe noted that the account holder had a Uganda Police Force warrant card in the name “Barigye William” and also wrote the same name on withdrawal slips.The court heard that PostBank received electronic funds transfers from the Bank of Uganda for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, including payments directed to account number 001030017010586, held in the name of Barigye William.The bank’s back-office manager, Norah Nagayi, testified that the bank credited the account in accordance with the instructions it received.She also told court that the bank did not receive any complaint from Barigye or his employer between December 2008 and June 2014 concerning the alleged anomaly.The complaint was only brought to the bank’s attention in August 2014, by which time the money had already been withdrawn.Justice Kinobe ruled that the bank could not reasonably have foreseen that the transactions were irregular, particularly because the account holder used the name “Barigye William” on the withdrawal slips.“It is clear from the foregoing that Barigye, the plaintiff, did not hold any account with Post Bank and so he had no relationship with the bank,” the judge ruled.The judge added that there was no relationship of proximity between Barigye and the bank, noting that PostBank owed a duty to release the money to its account holder upon request.He said the fact that the anomaly was raised in August 2014, long after the money had been withdrawn, meant that the bank could not be held liable for negligence.Justice Kinobe said had the trial magistrate properly considered the evidence and the letter from the Director of Citizenship and Immigration Control, she would not have found PostBank liable.He consequently allowed the appeal and set aside the chief magistrate’s judgment and all the orders issued on April 28, 2017.He ordered that each party bears its own costs of the appeal.","Justice Kinobe ruled that the bank could not reasonably have foreseen that the transactions were irregular, 06:50:00","Turkish defence textile firm eyes long-term partnership, local production in Uganda","turkish-defence-textile-firm-eyes-long-term-p","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">KAMPALA - \u003Cstrong>Türkiye is setting its sights on Uganda's growing defence and security market, with one of its leading military textile manufacturers signalling plans to move beyond product sales and explore local partnerships, skills transfer, and potentially production in the country.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Raff Military Textile, a Turkish manufacturer with more than eight decades of experience, is positioning Uganda as a strategic market as trade and economic relations between the two countries continue to deepen.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Speaking in an exclusive interview on Wednesday at Sheraton Hotel, the company's CEO, Eray Yükseloğlu, said Raff Military Textile is not interested in simply supplying off-the-shelf military uniforms and equipment but wants to build long-term relationships that could eventually strengthen local capacity.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We did not come to Uganda simply to sell products. We came to listen to Uganda, understand its needs, and build a long-term structure together,” Yükseloğlu said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>His comments come as Uganda continues to invest in security and defence, creating opportunities for manufacturers of military clothing, tactical equipment, boots, and protective gear.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Yükseloğlu said Raff's strength lies in its ability to tailor products to the specific needs of customers, rather than imposing a standard catalogue on different markets.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He said the company considers factors such as Uganda's climate, operating conditions, sizing requirements, fabric selection, colours, durability, and comfort before developing products.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/179ac8ba-4dba-4b10-9fbf-b7cc0557844f.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“The most important lesson from our experience in Africa is that the continent cannot be treated as a single market,” he said, noting that each country has different security priorities, procurement systems, and user expectations.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The company is also exploring opportunities to deepen its presence in Uganda. \u003Cstrong>Cyberattacks carried out by two OpenAI artificial intelligence models acting autonomously raise a novel legal question: who is responsible when AI goes rogue?\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>In mid-July, two OpenAI models undergoing testing left their confined environment — a scenario the developers had not anticipated — and ventured out onto the internet, attacking Hugging Face, an AI model-hosting platform.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue said Friday his company would not be pursuing legal action at this time.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He added Sunday that the US legal code has to be amended to address such groundbreaking incursions.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"We don't want to end up in a world where everyone is facing cyberattacks all the time because of agents and companies that are creating these agents,\" Delangue said on CBS News show \"Face the Nation.\"\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"So, I think it's important for regulators, for policymakers to think about the legal framework of this new kind of technology risk,\" he added.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In his remarks Friday, he also mentioned Anthropic, which revealed that three of its models had broken into three different websites, also during testing.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Negligence route\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Under US civil and criminal law, unauthorised access to a computer system is an offence.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"If a human OpenAI employee had broken into Hugging Face's systems... OpenAI would be liable for the employee's wrongful conduct,\" University of Houston law professor Gabriel Weil wrote in an opinion piece for the Transformer newsletter.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"When an AI agent does it, the law treats it very differently, at least for now,\" he added.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Matthew Tokson, a University of Utah law professor who focuses on new technologies, had a similar view, saying \"we haven't had to grapple with that being formed in anything that's not human, and I don't think courts are likely to be there yet.\"\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The question remains open, however, when it comes to the company that created the model.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Does 'we didn't tell the AI to do that' end the liability question?\" asked Rob T. Lee, head of research at the SANS cybersecurity training institute, in a post on X.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>University of Washington law professor Ryan Calo does not believe a criminal case would be likely to succeed.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"The company or individual would have to be at least reckless,\" he said, explaining they would \"be substantially certain the crime would occur and build or prompt the system anyway.\"\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Experts see greater potential for a civil — rather than criminal — case, where the burden of proof is lower.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Some people think that AI companies should be strictly liable if an AI agent that they deploy totally breaks out, causes damages,\" Tokson explained.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Others would prefer to do like a negligence assessment and see if they were actually negligent or if this was just sort of an unavoidable accident or something that couldn't possibly have been foreseen,\" he added.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In such cases, there is a standard of care in product design that judges or juries can use to make a ruling, Tokson continued.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"It's all a bit unwritten because we've never had an AI agent break out of its sandbox and hack other people on the internet before,\" he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>OpenAI could rely on the lack of legal precedent if it faced a lawsuit, but those that follow will no longer be able to do so, 22:29:18","Govt moves to commercialise homegrown digital innovations","govt-moves-to-commercialise-homegrown-digital","\u003Cp>________________\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">The Government has given technical teams at the Uganda Institute of Information and Communications Technology (UICT) two weeks to compile a comprehensive inventory of locally developed digital innovations and software that are ready for commercialisation.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The directive was issued by the Minister of State for ICT and National Guidance in charge of National Guidance, Alioni Yorke Odria, during his maiden familiarisation tour of the institute’s facilities in Nakawa, Kampala, on Friday (July 31).\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Odria, who is also the Aringa South MP, said the move is aimed at identifying promising innovations developed by Ugandan youth and creating pathways to take them from laboratories and innovation hubs into the marketplace.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The minister, who was appointed in the recent Cabinet reshuffle, replacing Godfrey Kabbyanga Baluku, commended UICT innovators for developing solutions with the potential to address local challenges and compete globally.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"I have given them two weeks to come up with a complete list of these new innovations, software and systems,\" Odria said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He added, \"We shall convene a workshop to review the innovations and engage government on mobilising resources to commercialise them, not only for Uganda but also for Africa and the rest of the world.\"\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Uganda has recorded several successful examples of homegrown innovations reaching commercial markets, including in e-mobility, financial technology, health technology and agro-processing.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In the automotive sector, Kiira Motors Corporation, which originated from research at Makerere University, has commercialised electric transit buses under the Kayoola E-Bus series, which are operating on public transport routes in Kampala and other corridors.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Electric mobility firms such as Zembo and Bodawerk have also expanded electric motorcycle solutions and battery-swapping networks targeting the East African boda-boda market.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>However, despite these successes, the broader innovation ecosystem continues to face challenges in moving ideas from research prototypes to commercially viable products.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>A key obstacle remains the gap between research and the market, with many innovations from academic and technical institutions struggling to secure intellectual property protection, manufacturing capacity, investment and industry partnerships needed for large-scale production.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>During his tour, Odria interacted with several innovations developed at UICT, including a virtual reality system at the institute’s innovation laboratory.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He also witnessed demonstrations of a digital monitoring system for the Parish Development Model (PDM), which provides real-time information on beneficiaries, funds disbursed, utilisation and loan repayments up to village level.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"They were able to pull out village beneficiaries in my own constituency,\" Odria said, adding, \"I could see how much money they had received, how they were utilising it and how they were paying it back. Everything is fully digitised.\"\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The minister was also shown an online business registration platform capable of completing company registration within an hour without applicants having to visit banks or queue at government offices.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Other innovations showcased included an artificial intelligence-powered self-driving vehicle prototype and a smart traffic management system developed by an eight-year-old innovator.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Odria said supporting locally developed technologies would be critical in achieving Uganda’s Vision 2040 ambition of transforming the country into a middle-income economy through innovation and digitalisation.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He added that digital systems can strengthen transparency and accountability in public service delivery by reducing opportunities for corruption.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The minister pledged government support to innovators through access to innovation hubs, high-speed internet, mentorship and other resources to help young Ugandans transform ideas into commercially successful products.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Dr. Dean Munene, the chairperson of the Governing Council at UICT, commended the strong partnership between the institute and government, saying the collaboration has contributed to the institute’s recent achievements.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Munene congratulated Odria on his official appointment, noting that the close working relationship between UICT, the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance, the Permanent Secretary, and other government stakeholders had been instrumental in advancing the institution’s mandate.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He said UICT remains central to Uganda’s digital transformation agenda through skills development, promotion of innovation, and supporting the country’s broader economic growth aspirations.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>While acknowledging operational and budgetary challenges facing the institute, Munene reaffirmed the Governing Council’s commitment to providing strategic leadership, strengthening governance structures, and ensuring accountability in the implementation of UICT’s mandate.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Dr. Amina Zawedde, the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance,  highlighted two key challenges affecting UICT: managing its wage bill and aligning its operations, particularly student admissions, with new statutory requirements.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Zawedde explained that UICT had initially relied on internally generated revenue to pay staff salaries before government, through the Ministry of Finance, agreed to take on part of the wage bill following engagements with the institute.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>However, she said the phased government intervention had created an absorption challenge, with UICT struggling to fully utilise the funds allocated for staff costs.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We started off with the institute depending on internally generated funds to pay for their staff. But we made a case to the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry took up part of the wage bill,” Zawedde said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She added that while the Government support was a significant milestone, the institute needed to address its capacity to absorb the funding provided.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>About UICT\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>UICT was founded in 2000 by the Uganda Communications Commission and later formally established and gazetted under Statutory Instrument Number 79 of October 2005. The institute is mandated to provide ICT human capital development, industry-relevant digital skilling, applied research, innovation and ICT advisory services.\u003C/p>","________________The 21:04:03","Uganda-Japan AI-POD Internship Project: Uganda students unveil AI tools","uganda-japan-ai-pod-internship-project-uganda","\u003Cp>________________\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">\u003Cstrong>At an interim report showcase held at Makerere University, nearly 40 students from three universities presented six AI-powered products built over three months under the Uganda-Japan AI-POD Internship Project.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The universities include: Makerere, the International University of East Africa (IUEA) and the Uganda Institute of Information and Communications Technology (UICT).\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The event drew officials from the Ministry of ICT and National Guidance, the National ICT Innovation Hub, Japanese firm Akademia, and Maarifasasa, a group that connects African talent to global markets.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Gen Suzuki, director of Akademia and the man behind the AI-POD concept, said the project grew out of a conviction that Uganda has the raw material Japan is desperately looking for. Akademia seeks to plug Japan’s growing tech talent shortage while lifting local engineers into global markets.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/bef07a68-e1e5-4836-ad5f-3fb468a86240.jpg\" alt=\"Gen Suzuki, director of Akademia makes his presentation during the event. (Photo by Ali Twaha)\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Gen Suzuki, director of Akademia makes his presentation during the event. (Photo by Ali Twaha)\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>“Uganda has talent. Intelligent, creative, eager to learn. The country’s youth are resourceful, and once they are given an opportunity, they are in position to support the growth of the economy. AI-POD can support Uganda,” he said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>What started as a plan for 12 interns ballooned into a cohort of 38 students working across six groups, building tools ranging from an AI translation checker that catches errors in cross-border communication, to an AI recruiter that conducts job interviews around the clock, to 3D AI avatars designed to give digital services a human face.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Officials said the AI-POD tools are moving toward real use. Akademia says the translation checker and several other products are ready for trial testing, while the daily activity reporting system built for tracking work on outsourced projects is already cleared for business use.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Robert Bob Okello, founder of Maarifasasa, said Uganda’s talent must prepare and be ready when the opportunities present themselves.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We have the opportunity right now. 10:13:00","Uganda becomes East Africa's hub for virus detection and research","uganda-becomes-east-africas-hub-for-virus-det","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">KAMPALA -\u003Cstrong> Uganda has strengthened its regional leadership in infectious disease surveillance after the Uganda Virus Research Institute (UVRI) was officially designated the East African Community (EAC) Regional Centre of Excellence in Virology.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The Centre, launched in Entebbe on Wednesday, July 22, will serve as the region's hub for advanced virology emerging and re-emerging viral diseases.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The launch was officiated by Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja, who represented President Yoweri Museveni during celebrations marking UVRI's 90th anniversary.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Nabbanja said the designation places greater responsibility on Uganda and the region to strengthen health security amid evolving disease threats.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"The world is changing rapidly alongside evolving health demands and policies. Through this journey, we have seen and learnt that a nation that studies its own pathogens is a self-reliant nation. We commit to increasing funding for research,\" she said.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>She noted that the Centre would not only benefit Uganda but also strengthen regional collaboration in responding to disease outbreaks that easily spread across borders.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/93f22552-007d-465f-8a5d-38759d389b60.jpg\" alt=\"Nabbanja said the designation places greater responsibility on Uganda and the region to strengthen health security amid evolving disease threats. We mobilised resources, and today we are proud to hand over this donation to the school management,” Tumusiime said.Deogratious Ssekyole, the Mpigi district education officer, applauded the Rotarians for the generous gesture, noting that public-private partnerships are vital to achieving sustainable development goals in the education sector and called on the school management to guard the donation given to them jealously. On behalf of the school management committee, Rev Canon Nkambo Mugerwa thanked the Rotarians for their philanthropic spirit and assured donors that the community would protect the investments. The school Headteacher, Deborah Nampeewo, expressed profound relief, stating that the in-house photocopying machine would slash administrative printing costs, which will allow the school to reallocate scarce resources to other academic needs.","\"Parents must stop abandoning their core responsibilities. 19:47:28","Dutch students unveil 'world-first' solar-powered ambulance","dutch-students-unveil-world-first-solar-power","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">BARNEVELD - \u003Cstrong>A Dutch student team on Tuesday unveiled what they believe to be the world's first solar-powered ambulance, which they hope can bring much-needed medical care to the remotest parts of the globe.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The sleek, futuristic-looking, white and yellow vehicle boasts solar panels on the roof that power its engine but also medical devices from x-ray machines to defibrillators.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The two-seater ambulance, named Stella Juva, can reach a top speed of 120 kilometres per hour (75 miles per hour) and is designed for inaccessible off-road terrain.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>With a range of 715 kilometres on a sunny day, the car has a solar power-charged battery to ensure the vehicle and equipment works at night or when it is cloudy.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"Stella Juva is fully equipped to deliver medical healthcare in hard-to-reach areas,\" said project leader Mathijs van Gerven, a 21-year-old student of biomedical engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The vehicle is designed to bring healthcare to the patient, rather than transport them to hospitals. 17:28:36","Let the machine type; teach our children to think","let-the-machine-type-teach-our-children-to-th","\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">____________\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"text-decoration: underline;\">\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">OPINION\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">\u003Cem>Dr Richard Kimera (PhD)\u003C/em>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The world's most powerful AI bosses say software now writes itself. In Uganda, where the median age is about 17, that has students and parents asking whether a computer science degree is still worth the fees. It is. But only if we learn the right lesson.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>A Senior Six student at Masaka Secondary School recently put a question to me that I have heard, in different words, a dozen times this year: “If the computer can now write the programs by itself, why should I waste four years and my parents' money studying software engineering?”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>It is a fair question, and it deserves a fair answer, not the comforting one, and not the frightening one, but the true one.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">First, the part that is real\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>Let me begin with what is real, because pretending otherwise insults the reader.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In March 2025, at a Council on Foreign Relations event in the United States, Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, one of the companies building the most advanced AI in the world, predicted that within three to six months, machines would be “writing 90 percent of the code,” and within a year, essentially all of it. \u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>A year earlier, at a government summit in Dubai, Jensen Huang, head of the chip giant Nvidia whose hardware powers much of this revolution, went further and told young people to stop learning to code altogether. The future programming language, he argued, “is human”, you would simply tell the computer what you want in plain words.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>These are not village rumours. They are the considered words of the people who profit most from the technology. And the hiring numbers have begun to echo them: worldwide, openings for junior, entry-level programmers have fallen by more than half since 2022, and a study from Stanford University found that employment among the youngest developers, aged 22 to 25, has dropped by roughly a fifth from its peak.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>So the fear in that Masaka classroom is not foolish. It is arriving.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Now, the lesson almost everyone gets wrong\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003C/strong>Here is where the conversation goes off the road. People hear “the machine can write code” and conclude “so there is nothing left to learn.” That is precisely the wrong lesson, and if our young people swallow it, we will have talked an entire generation out of becoming the one thing most worth becoming.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Read those same experts more carefully. Even Amodei, in the very breath he used to predict 90 percent, added a caveat the headlines ignored: a human must still decide what the program is for, set its conditions, and make the design decisions. Even Huang, having told children not to code, immediately insisted that we must instead upskill everyone. The machine writes the lines. It does not decide what is worth building, or whether what it built is right.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>That distinction is everything.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">What these tools actually are\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Strip away the mystery, and an AI coding tool is something like the fastest, most confident boda rider in Kampala. Tell it where you want to go and it will get you there at remarkable speed. But it does not know the city the way you do. If you cannot read the map yourself, if you have never walked the streets, you cannot tell when it is taking you the long way, driving you toward a swamp, or speeding with total confidence in entirely the wrong direction.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>To someone who knows the city, that rider is a gift. To someone who knows nothing, the very same rider is a danger dressed up as convenience.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">How an AI agent actually writes code\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>It helps to look under the bonnet, because the magic dissolves on inspection.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>At the centre of these tools sits a large language model, a system trained on enormous amounts of text and code to do one narrow thing extremely well: predict the next chunk of text that should follow. It has no grasp of your business, your users, or the law. It has patterns.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>An “agent” wraps that model in a loop. Give it a goal and it does roughly this. First it breaks the goal into smaller steps, this is called planning. Then it writes a piece of code for the first step and runs that code in a sandbox, an isolated space where the program can execute without touching anything important. It reads whatever comes back, a result, or an error message, and feeds that back into itself to choose the next move. \u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Reason, act, observe; reason, act, observe, again and again, keeping a short memory of what it has already tried so it does not go in circles. It can also reach out to tools: call an internet service, query a database, open a file. The code it produces along the way is disposable scaffolding, written to get an answer, then often thrown away. As one recent research paper frames it, the code is no longer the product; the agent itself is.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>That is genuinely powerful. It is also why its failures are the kind that bite. The model is straining to produce code that looks right and passes the immediate test, not code that is correct in every situation it will later meet. It can write a function that handles the example you gave it and quietly mishandles the one you did not: a customer with no middle name, a transaction at midnight on the last day of the financial year, a mobile network that drops halfway through a payment. The agent will report success. Only a human who understands the system will know where to look for the rot.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>The cliff the machines fall off\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>This is not my hunch. A research paper posted this June to arXiv, an online archive where scientists share findings before formal peer review, by Zhenfeng Cao, a researcher in China, lays out this new “agentic” way of building software and then tests where it breaks. Drawing on a careful set of trials known as EvoClaw, it found something that should be pinned to the wall of every computer lab in East Africa.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>When AI agents are handed small, neat, self-contained tasks, they succeed more than eight times out of ten. But when they are asked to do what real software actually demands, keep a living system running over time, where today's change must not break what was built last month, and where small early mistakes quietly multiply, their success collapses to below four in ten.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The bigger, messier, and more consequential the system, the more it needs a human being who genuinely understands it.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>The tool can fool even the experts\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>You might think the danger is only for beginners. It is not. In a careful controlled trial, the research group METR found that experienced open-source developers using AI assistance were actually about 19 percent slower, even as they felt faster. Other reviews report that AI written code carries more bugs and gets rewritten more often than code thought through by a person. The tool feels quick while quietly costing you. That is the trap.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>We have seen a smaller version of it before. A student who masters the calculator but never learned arithmetic cannot tell when the screen shows nonsense because a zero was mistyped. The calculator did not make him careless; skipping the foundations did. AI is now a calculator for almost everything, and the temptation to skip the foundations has never been stronger, or more expensive.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cstrong>And our most important systems are not toys\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>What are our most consequential systems? The mobile money platforms that move a vast share of this country's money. The systems behind URA, NSSF, the hospitals, the banks, the Electoral Commission. These are not classroom exercises. In Uganda, where the median age is about 17, that has students and parents asking whether a computer science degree is still worth the fees. It is. But only if we learn the right lesson.A Senior Six student at Masaka Secondary School recently put a question to me that I have heard, in different words, a dozen times this year: “If the computer can now write the programs by itself, why should I waste four years and my parents' money studying software engineering?”It is a fair question, and it deserves a fair answer, not the comforting one, and not the frightening one, but the true one.First, the part that is realLet me begin with what is real, because pretending otherwise insults the reader.In March 2025, at a Council on Foreign Relations event in the United States, Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, one of the companies building the most advanced AI in the world, predicted that within three to six months, machines would be “writing 90 percent of the code,” and within a year, essentially all of it. A year earlier, at a government summit in Dubai, Jensen Huang, head of the chip giant Nvidia whose hardware powers much of this revolution, went further and told young people to stop learning to code altogether. The future programming language, he argued, “is human”, you would simply tell the computer what you want in plain words.These are not village rumours. They are the considered words of the people who profit most from the technology. And the hiring numbers have begun to echo them: worldwide, openings for junior, entry-level programmers have fallen by more than half since 2022, and a study from Stanford University found that employment among the youngest developers, aged 22 to 25, has dropped by roughly a fifth from its peak.So the fear in that Masaka classroom is not foolish. It is arriving.Now, the lesson almost everyone gets wrongHere is where the conversation goes off the road. People hear “the machine can write code” and conclude “so there is nothing left to learn.” That is precisely the wrong lesson, and if our young people swallow it, we will have talked an entire generation out of becoming the one thing most worth becoming.Read those same experts more carefully. Even Amodei, in the very breath he used to predict 90 percent, added a caveat the headlines ignored: a human must still decide what the program is for, set its conditions, and make the design decisions. Even Huang, having told children not to code, immediately insisted that we must instead upskill everyone. The machine writes the lines. It does not decide what is worth building, or whether what it built is right.That distinction is everything.What these tools actually areStrip away the mystery, and an AI coding tool is something like the fastest, most confident boda rider in Kampala. Tell it where you want to go and it will get you there at remarkable speed. But it does not know the city the way you do. If you cannot read the map yourself, if you have never walked the streets, you cannot tell when it is taking you the long way, driving you toward a swamp, or speeding with total confidence in entirely the wrong direction.To someone who knows the city, that rider is a gift. To someone who knows nothing, the very same rider is a danger dressed up as convenience.How an AI agent actually writes codeIt helps to look under the bonnet, because the magic dissolves on inspection.At the centre of these tools sits a large language model, a system trained on enormous amounts of text and code to do one narrow thing extremely well: predict the next chunk of text that should follow. It has no grasp of your business, your users, or the law. It has patterns.An “agent” wraps that model in a loop. Give it a goal and it does roughly this. First it breaks the goal into smaller steps, this is called planning. Then it writes a piece of code for the first step and runs that code in a sandbox, an isolated space where the program can execute without touching anything important. It reads whatever comes back, a result, or an error message, and feeds that back into itself to choose the next move. Reason, act, observe; reason, act, observe, again and again, keeping a short memory of what it has already tried so it does not go in circles. It can also reach out to tools: call an internet service, query a database, open a file. The code it produces along the way is disposable scaffolding, written to get an answer, then often thrown away. As one recent research paper frames it, the code is no longer the product; the agent itself is.That is genuinely powerful. It is also why its failures are the kind that bite. The model is straining to produce code that looks right and passes the immediate test, not code that is correct in every situation it will later meet. It can write a function that handles the example you gave it and quietly mishandles the one you did not: a customer with no middle name, a transaction at midnight on the last day of the financial year, a mobile network that drops halfway through a payment. The agent will report success. Only a human who understands the system will know where to look for the rot.The cliff the machines fall offThis is not my hunch. A research paper posted this June to arXiv, an online archive where scientists share findings before formal peer review, by Zhenfeng Cao, a researcher in China, lays out this new “agentic” way of building software and then tests where it breaks. Drawing on a careful set of trials known as EvoClaw, it found something that should be pinned to the wall of every computer lab in East Africa.When AI agents are handed small, neat, self-contained tasks, they succeed more than eight times out of ten. But when they are asked to do what real software actually demands, keep a living system running over time, where today's change must not break what was built last month, and where small early mistakes quietly multiply, their success collapses to below four in ten.The bigger, messier, and more consequential the system, the more it needs a human being who genuinely understands it.The tool can fool even the expertsYou might think the danger is only for beginners. It is not. In a careful controlled trial, the research group METR found that experienced open-source developers using AI assistance were actually about 19 percent slower, even as they felt faster. Other reviews report that AI written code carries more bugs and gets rewritten more often than code thought through by a person. The tool feels quick while quietly costing you. That is the trap.We have seen a smaller version of it before. A student who masters the calculator but never learned arithmetic cannot tell when the screen shows nonsense because a zero was mistyped. The calculator did not make him careless; skipping the foundations did. AI is now a calculator for almost everything, and the temptation to skip the foundations has never been stronger, or more expensive.And our most important systems are not toysWhat are our most consequential systems? The mobile money platforms that move a vast share of this country's money. The systems behind URA, NSSF, the hospitals, the banks, the Electoral Commission. These are not classroom exercises. They are exactly the places where a confident, plausible-looking error, the kind these tools produce most easily, can cost money, trust, or lives.Benoni Katende, the chief technology officer at NSSF, put the real job plainly at a tech showcase in Kampala: find a genuine problem, and use technology to solve it, faster, cheaper, better. Notice what that demands. Not faster typing. Understanding deep enough to know which problem matters and whether the solution actually works.Why this is Uganda's moment, not Uganda's threatHere is the striking thing. She has presented herself, even as a seasoned professor, as someone who must constantly learn, unlearn and relearn. We are also discussing using our labs at the border,” Kaleebu said.During the July celebrations, UVRI will also launch a new World Health Organisation-accredited polio sequencing laboratory aimed at supporting global efforts to eradicate polio.Kaleebu said the institute had worked on polio research and vaccines since the 1960s and had now been selected as a reference laboratory for sequencing vaccine-derived polio strains.“We think we are towards the end of polio, and we hope the lab will contribute to eradication efforts,” he said.Push for African-led scienceMakerere University Lung Institute Director and Chief Research Scientist Dr Bruce Kirenga said UVRI’s survival and scientific contribution over the last 90 years demonstrated the importance of investing in African-led science and research institutions.Kirenga said Uganda and Africa needed to move beyond simply identifying viruses and begin developing homegrown medical solutions, including vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics.“At this point, the issue of science sovereignty is very important for Africans. Whatever little effort we are doing in our small institutes and laboratories can be done in any other lab, and they send us the results and everything. But we must be seeing ourselves,” Kirenga said, adding, “We need to go beyond describing these pathogens but also be able to create local medical solutions because these solutions will reach our people faster.”Kirenga revealed that Ugandan scientists were already collaborating with UVRI on promising Ebola-related innovations ranging from diagnostics to vaccines, although he declined to disclose details.He welcomed ongoing discussions for UVRI to become a degree-awarding institution under Makerere University, saying the move would strengthen scientific training and research capacity in Uganda.Ebola contextThe announcement comes at a time Uganda is battling the Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease that broke out in the neighbouring DR Congo. standard.\u003C/strong>\u003C/span>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Opposition leader Arvind Kejriwal marched towards Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence carrying petitions signed by more than 200,000 people, but was stopped by police before reaching his destination.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>India, the world's third-largest auto market, says the biofuel move is helping curb dependence on imported crude and boost farm incomes.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>But motorists have voiced concerns over vehicle performance, and the government's campaign has upset India's vast middle class -- a key voter base for Modi, who worry that they are being forced to shoulder the costs of the transition.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>AFP breaks down the speed bumps on India's fuel blending road.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">What's ethanol-blended petrol?\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>E20, the fuel at the centre of the controversy, is essentially petrol mixed with 20 percent ethanol -- which is produced largely from sugarcane.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>India has flirted with the idea of biofuels for decades, primarily because it depends on other countries for over 80 percent of its crude oil requirements.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Over the last decade, Modi's government has accelerated the biofuel programme, with ethanol blending going from less than 1.5 percent in 2013-14 to 20 percent in 2025-26.\u003Cbr>This has allowed India to save roughly $20 billion in foreign exchange since 2014-15 and boosted farmer incomes by $16.4 billion in the same period, government figures show.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Why are drivers concerned?\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Many motorists fear that the E20 petrol blend will harm engines and raise maintenance costs in vehicles designed for lower ethanol blends.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>A flurry of videos showcasing alleged damage to vehicle parts and drops in mileage have gone viral on social media in recent months.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Political analyst Tehseen Poonawalla, who led a street protest against E20 last month, has accused the government of rushing the nationwide rollout while dismissing legitimate public concerns.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The government has acknowledged that E20 could lead to a small dip in fuel efficiency -- in the range of 3 percent to 5 percent -- but has rejected allegations of engine damage.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Junior Oil Minister Suresh Gopi told parliament last week that more than 200 million two-wheelers and 300 million cars had operated on E20 without any \"verified evidence of widespread engine failures or vehicle breakdowns\".\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The government has also cited manufacturer data over the last year to state that \"no E20-linked corrosion, abnormal wear or reduction in component life\" was reported, even in vehicles not originally designed for the blend.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>India's road transport minister, Nitin Gadkari, has cited a study that suggested some older vehicles may require replacement of rubber components and gaskets, but argued such work could be \"easily managed during routine servicing\".\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">What are car companies saying?\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>India's auto industry has largely supported the government.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Officials at Maruti Suzuki, the country's largest car manufacturer, have said the company's testing of E20 fuel on vehicles designed for E10 showed no areas of concern.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>And one of the biggest domestic producers of motorcycles, Hero MotoCorp, says its own service data showed no incidence of higher damage in vehicles running on E20 compared to older fuels.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Some automakers have warned against misinformation.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Toyota India said issues raised in a viral complaint were caused by fuel contamination and \"not related to E20 fuel usage\".\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">What next?\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Critics have asked the government to offer signs of relenting.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In a statement last month, India's oil ministry said that offering multiple options at the pump would be logistically difficult and they are being forced to shoulder the costs of the transition.AFP breaks down the speed bumps on India's fuel blending road.What's ethanol-blended petrol?E20, the fuel at the centre of the controversy, is essentially petrol mixed with 20 percent ethanol -- which is produced largely from sugarcane.India has flirted with the idea of biofuels for decades, primarily because it depends on other countries for over 80 percent of its crude oil requirements.Over the last decade, Modi's government has accelerated the biofuel programme, with ethanol blending going from less than 1.5 percent in 2013-14 to 20 percent in 2025-26.This has allowed India to save roughly $20 billion in foreign exchange since 2014-15 and boosted farmer incomes by $16.4 billion in the same period, government figures show.Why are drivers concerned?Many motorists fear that the E20 petrol blend will harm engines and raise maintenance costs in vehicles designed for lower ethanol blends.A flurry of videos showcasing alleged damage to vehicle parts and drops in mileage have gone viral on social media in recent months.Political analyst Tehseen Poonawalla, who led a street protest against E20 last month, has accused the government of rushing the nationwide rollout while dismissing legitimate public concerns.The government has acknowledged that E20 could lead to a small dip in fuel efficiency -- in the 15:01:00","Is Karamoja’s broken pastoralism fueling migration to cities?","is-karamojas-broken-pastoralism-fueling-migra","\u003Cp>\u003Cbr>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">KARAMOJA \u003C/span>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 14pt;\">- As dawn breaks over Kampala, Peter Lokuta is already searching the streets of Kisenyi for scrap metal. He moves through rubbish piles, construction sites, and roadside dumps, knowing every hour matters. In the city, one person’s waste has become another’s livelihood.\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“It is backbreaking work,” he said. “But every drop of sweat keeps food on my table. I would rather live by the sweat of my brow than stretch out my hand to beg.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For Lokuta, life has changed dramatically. Born into the Karimojong pastoralist community, where cattle represent wealth, security, and identity, he now searches Kampala’s streets for discarded metal instead of grazing livestock.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As Lokuta speaks, images of Karamoja’s endless plains come to mind—a harsh yet beautiful landscape shaped by resilience. He left one struggle behind only to face another. The spear has given way to a sack of scrap metal, but survival remains the battle defining his days.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>His story unfolds in Kisenyi, one of Kampala’s most crowded neighbourhoods, where narrow alleys, packed homes, and daily struggles define life as residents seek survival.\u003Cbr>In this bug-infested neighbourhood, Lokiru’s struggle reflects Kampala’s slum reality, where survival is costly, and only air seems free.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“It is not easy to find affordable food in Kampala, but this place (Kisenyi) serves meals for as little as Sh2,000,” he says. “With Sh5,000, you can eat like a king.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>However, even eating comes with expenses that many people in rural areas rarely think about.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For Lokiru, a meal brings another cost: a trip to a pay-per-use toilet, where even basic needs require money in Kisenyi.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As Lokiru went about his daily struggles, one question kept returning to mind: Why would people leave rural homes with toilets, proper drainage, and healthier surroundings for a life in the city where they are packed like sardines?\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For Lokiru, life changed forever when his father was killed in a brutal raid that also stripped the family of their most valuable asset—their cattle.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In Karamoja, losing cattle can mean losing everything. Livestock is often the foundation upon which families build their lives, and without it, survival becomes uncertain.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>His escape began on foot to Soroti. There, he teamed up with a group of young people bound for Kampala. Together, they travelled through Mbale and Jinja before reaching Kisenyi in Kampala.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“I know East or West, home is best,” he says. “I want to get capital for business and then settle in Mbale or Soroti or Moroto, where I can easily keep an eye on home.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>His words carry both ambition and longing. Though Kampala provides a livelihood, his thoughts remain tied to home and to a future that might one day bring him closer to it.\u003Cbr>Seeking to understand how Karimojong migrants have adapted to life in Kisenyi, I spoke to the LC1 chairperson for Kasaato zone, Godfrey Kakande.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Kakande, many who arrived from Karamoja have gradually become urbanites. “We experienced a clash of cultures because many Karimojong feared using toilets, believing it would prevent them from bearing children,” said Kakande, adding that this created conflict with their neighbours.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The transition was not always smooth. Deeply held beliefs sometimes collided with the demands of urban living, creating tensions between newcomers and long-time residents.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Alongside the Karamojong immigrants, Kisenyi is home to urban refugees from Somalia. Kampala’s refugee population also includes Ethiopians and Eritreans on Gaba Road.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/7f179e81-b01c-4dc3-9e65-3cdd599c31b9.jpg\" alt=\"Cattle struggling to get water for drinking du to drought in Kotido district, Karamoja Sub-County, recently.\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>Cattle struggling to get water for drinking du to drought in Kotido district, Karamoja Sub-County, recently.\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cbr>Lokuta’s roots\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>To understand why more people are leaving northeastern Uganda for towns and cities, I retraced Peter Lokuta’s journey to Lomarotoit Village, Iriri Sub-county, Napak, where his story began.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Napak is one of the nine districts in Karamoja. It borders Abim and Kotido to the northwest and Moroto to the north and northeast and Katakwi to the south. Nakapiripirit and Nabilatuk to the southeast, Otuke to the west, and Amuria to the southwest.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The boda-boda rider taking me from Katakwi town to Iriri became my first guide into this world. As we bounced along dusty roads, he spoke passionately about his homeland.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>This, he said, is a land of pastoralists and agro-pastoralists, a place where livestock, agriculture, and mining coexist. Beneath its rugged surface lie some of the much-sought-after gold.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Clouds of dust swirled across the plains and followed us for miles, as if announcing our arrival. By the time I reached Iriri village, where Lokuta is regarded as a son of the soil, a thick layer of dust had settled on my clothes, turning my shirt brown.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As I settled onto a round, three-legged stool beneath the unforgiving Karamoja sun, another reality emerged. Hidden beneath the dusty landscape were deeper and more painful struggles: a persistent water crisis and growing food insecurity.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>I had carried bottled water with me. After washing my face, I was suddenly surrounded by young children and desperate faces pleading for a sip. When I shared what remained, a scramble broke out around the bottle.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In that moment, the phrase “water is life” took on a meaning far beyond words. “We live in a land of scarcity, but the disappearance of water and the worsening hunger crisis have made life even harder,” Michael Lorot, Chairperson of Lomarotoit Village, said, pausing as he gazed across the vast plains stretching towards the horizon.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For a brief moment, I wondered whether he was staring at an invisible enemy. Was danger lurking somewhere in the distance? Was a rival clan preparing an attack?\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“This is our land, given to us by God and passed down by our ancestors. But we face immense pressure from a hostile environment, including climate change. The modern world has arrived; mining has also come with profiteers.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>His words captured the challenge facing many communities across Karamoja—a struggle not against a visible enemy, but against forces that are steadily changing the land on which their lives depend.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Precious cattle\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>In this remote corner of northeastern Uganda, the relationship between people, land, and cattle runs deeper than economics.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Lorot, this bond is known as pastoralism, a system that has shaped generations of Karimojong families and communities.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>People here do not simply own livestock. Their lives are intertwined with their animals and the land that sustains them.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Pastoralism has survived for centuries through mobility, resilience, and environmental knowledge, enabling communities to endure droughts, changing seasons, and harsh climatic conditions.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>While some dismiss them as wanderers, local leaders insist their movements have always followed established patterns.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Lorot explained that seasonal migration was carefully organised and guided by elders. Communities sought consent before moving beyond their traditional territories and understood the landscape in remarkable detail.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“We used to move in the dry season and get good pastures and water,” he says, adding that they knew the landscape like the back of their hand.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cimg src=\"https://newvision-media.s3.amazonaws.com/cms/af2f7f92-df4c-427f-abbe-5dfeaeeeaedc.jpg\" alt=\"\" width=\"100%\" height=\"100%\">\u003Cp>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cem>\u003Csmall>\u003C/small>\u003C/em>\u003C/strong>\u003C/p>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">\u003Cbr>Situation analysis\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>For generations, these movements ensured that livestock survived harsh seasons and communities remained food secure.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Lorot, population growth and climate change are intensifying competition for water and pasture resources that are becoming increasingly scarce.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“It is a different ball game,” Lorot said. “When a severe dry spell or drought strikes, pastoralists are forced to move in search of water and pasture.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Traditional migratory corridors are steadily disappearing as communal land is divided and transferred into private ownership. Routes that livestock once followed freely are being blocked, narrowing the options available to pastoralists, according to Lorot. He complained that rampant land grabbing is encroaching on their ancestral grazing lands.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As herders move into restricted areas, conflicts often follow. The result is that communities are increasingly confined to smaller spaces, limiting the flexibility that has long been the backbone of pastoralism.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Dr. Sidonia Angom Ochieng and the Karamoja Peace and Technology University, this growing restriction threatens far more than livestock production. “It threatens a way of life. Pastoralism is not only an economic activity. It is closely linked to cultural identity, stability, and community cohesion,” she says.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>According to Isaac Kabongo, the executive director of the Ecological Christian Organisation (ECO), significant numbers of people are now leaving Karamoja for other parts of Uganda.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He notes that migration is also occurring elsewhere in the country, with communities from southwestern Uganda increasingly moving into the midwestern region.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“There are pastoralists who once moved only within Karamoja, but they are now migrating to other parts of the country,” said Kabongo.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Dr. Callist Tindimugaya, the Commissioner for Water Resources Planning and Regulation at the Ministry of Water and Environment, agrees.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Floods, landslides, and declining resources are forcing people, including Balaalo herders, to leave homes and seek alternatives elsewhere,” said Tindimugaya.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Cross-border migration\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>As competition for scarce resources intensifies, migrants often encounter settled communities, creating tensions and conflict in areas such as eastern and northern Uganda.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Climate change is affecting many areas in different ways. There are areas that are prone to the changing climate, which is behind the droughts that are becoming frequent and intense. Soil fertility has gone down. Climate change is affecting agriculture and fertility. When water is reduced, people move. Water is critical to human survival, observes Tindimugaya.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>In Karamoja, Kabongo says, widespread food insecurity is increasingly pushing people into towns. “They are being displaced and are seeking livelihoods in urban areas, where there is little or no land,” said Kabongo.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The trend reflects the combined effects of climate change and the disruption of pastoralism, a system that has long provided food, employment, and wealth in the region.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\"When pasture or other resources become scarce, conflicts emerge,” said Kabongo, adding that such disputes sometimes spill across national borders. “As I speak, Pokot pastoralists from Kenya have crossed into Amudat and have little respect for the territorial boundaries of other communities.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>The impacts of climate change are more severe in north-eastern Kenya than in Uganda. As a result, the Pokot and Turkana migrate into Uganda when prolonged dry spells hit the region.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Uganda’s average temperature has risen by 1.3°C since the 1960s, bringing more heat stress, longer dry spells, and recurring droughts for agro-pastoral communities, according to the World Bank.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>A publication titled “From Vision to Action: Uganda Launches a Climate Resilience Initiative in the Cattle Corridor” notes that Uganda’s cattle corridor, which covers about half the country, is being hit harder by climate impacts than other regions.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>\u003Cstrong>\u003Cspan style=\"font-size: 18pt;\">Way forward\u003Cbr>\u003C/span>\u003C/strong>\u003Cbr>The Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD) Protocol on Transhumance supports orderly cross-border pastoral movement to reduce resource conflicts and protect livelihoods. Uganda supports the IGAD Protocol on Transhumance but has neither signed nor ratified it.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>Pastoralists searching for water and pasture often clash with settled communities, triggering conflicts, says Advocates Coalition for Environment and Development Deputy Executive Director Onesmus Mugyenyi.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“Climate change forces people to move in search of alternative livelihoods. It also intensifies competition for scarce resources,” he observes.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>For Mugyenyi, adaptation is the way to go. “We need to adapt because we cannot run away from climate change,” he said, adding, “It is important to respond to climate change by diversifying opportunities.”\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>He pointed to value addition, irrigation expansion, and strengthening resilience to climate shocks as solutions to climate change.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>A study led by United Nations Framework to Combat Climate Change climate negotiator Fred Onduri informed Uganda's new migration policy to manage climate change-driven mobility.\u003Cbr>\u003Cbr>“It came up with information regarding where people are moving. will provide access to an expanded market of hundreds of millions of consumers. added.\u003C/p>\u003Cp data-start=\"3819\" data-end=\"4140\"> \u003C/p>\u003Ch3 data-section-id=\"1ynta7b\" data-start=\"4142\" data-end=\"4202\">How EAGC is supporting members to meet quality data-start=\"4391\" data-end=\"4588\"> \u003C/p>\u003Cp data-start=\"4590\" data-end=\"4800\">In terms of accreditation, he said EAGC has been accredited as an ISO 9000:2015 inspection body,
